subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I promised the house a few days ago that I would endeavour to-day to make a statement with respect to the Beauharnois undertaking, and that the government would endeavour to consider the matter carefully on Saturday last so that the statement might be as complete as possible. I shall have to ask the indulgence of the house for it is necessary for me to read documents of considerable length.
1.	The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company is a creature of the Quebec legislature. It was incorporated in 1902, and its charter was amended in 1910, 1928 and 1930. It is therefore not a corporation over which the parliament of Canada has legislative jurisdiction.
2.	The Beauharnois Power Corporation is an entity created under the provisions of the Companies Act of Canada. It is a corporation over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction.
3.	In 1929 the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited undertook to create and sell $30,000,000 thirty-year six per cent collateral trust sinking fund bonds. These bonds were to be dated the first day of October, 1929, and were therefore payable in 1959. These bonds were secured, not as some persons have assumed, by a charge against the undertaking,
but by a mortgage on the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company Limited, and the Beauharnois Transmission Company, and the Beauharnois Land Company, and the Beauharnois Construction Company-all as mentioned in the second schedule to the deed of trust given by the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited to the Royal Trust Company as trustee. The schedule to which I have referred is printed on page 75 of that document, and in order that there may be no misunderstanding with respect to the matter, I shall read the schedule:
39.989	(thirty-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine) shares of a par value of $100 each of the capital stock of said Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, being all the outstanding shares of the capital stock of said company, except eleven (11) shares held by the directors thereof:
49.989	(forty-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine) shares (having no nominal or par value) of said Beauharnois Construction Company, being all the outstanding shares of the capital stock of said company, except eleven (11) shares held by the directors thereof;
49.989	(forty-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine) shares (having no nominal or par value) of said Beauharnois Transmission Company, being all the outstanding shares of the capital stock of said company, except eleven (11) shares held by the directors thereof;
49.989	(forty-nine thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine) shares (having no nominal or par value) of said Beauharnois Land Company, being all the outstanding shares of the capital stock of the said company, except eleven (11) shares held by the directors thereof.
These shares constituted the security upon which the issue of collateral trust bonds was based. The provisions as to the amount of the proceeds arising from the sale of the bonds to be received by the Quebec company, the parent company, The Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, are indicated by a document dated the twentieth day of November, 1929, being an agreement made between the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited and the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. That document provides not only for the issue of the $30,000,000 of securities; but it also provides for what the operating or parent company was to receive from this issue, the figures being $22,500,000. Section 6 reads * as follows:
The corporation hereby undertakes and agrees to create and issue an issue of thirty year six per cent collateral trust sinking fund bonds of an aggregate principle amount of $30,000,000, and out of the proceeds thereof to make advances by way of loan from time to time to the company up to an amount of $22,250,000 as the same may be required from time to time by the company for any of the following purposes, namely:
(a)	for the payment of any of the obligations and liabilities assumed by the corpora-
2104	COMMONS
Beauhamois Power-Mr. Bennett
tion under the said agreement dated the 31st day of October, 1929, between the corporation and the Beauharnois power syndicate, which obligations and liabilities -are hereby assumed by the company as hereinafter set forth, or
(b)	for the payment of expenditures from time to time made or proposed to be made, either by the company or by any subsidiary company or companies of the company, for or in connection -with the development or marketing of hydro electric power resulting from the difference in level between lake St. Francis and lake St. Louis in the province of Quebec, Canada, including therein but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, taxes, rates and assessments, governmental fees and duties and overhead and other expenses of the company and of any of its subsidiary companies, and expenditures for the acquisition of properties and rights of any and all kinds in connection therewith; or
(c)	for such other corporate purposes of the company as the corporation may approve.
Provided however that any of the said $22,250,000 applied by the corporation in* payment of interest on the said $30,000,000 of thirty year six per cent collateral trust sinking fund bonds of the corporation, up to and including the interest payable on the 1st day of October, 1931, shall be deemed to have been advanced under this section 6 to the company by the corporation and to have been paid by the company pursuant to the provisions of section 9 (a) hereof. The corporation further undertakes and agrees to credit the company in the manner set out in section 9 hereof with an amount equal to the net income directly or indirectly received by the corporation on the portion of the said $22,250,000 from time to time remaining unadvanced to the company.
It will be observed from what I have just read that it is provided that the corporation was also to assume the obligations of the Light, Heat and Power Company in connection with the syndicate to which reference has been made so frequently. Those payments so far as one can ascertain amounted to nearly $4,000,000. So that the sum left, $22,500,000 was to be depleted by that further amount. It was also provided alike by agreement and by trust deed, as will be found at .page 38 of that document, that the moneys paid to the trustee upon the certification of bonds shall be available for the payment of interest until October 1, 1931. As the interest amounted to, it will be observed, $1,800,000 per annum, two years interest in round figures were also to come out of proceeds of the bonds, amounting in all to approximately $3,600,000.
4.	The next point I desire to direct attention to is the prospectuses that were issued for the sale of these securities. They were issued by many bond dealers throughout Canada, the one I hold in my hand being issued by Wood, Gundy and Company and providing that there should be an issue of first mortgage securities for the purpose of completing the undertaking, because it will 
be Obvious from what I have just read that the relatively small sum remaining out of the $30,000 000 collateral trust bonds would not be sufficient to complete the undertaking. In this prospectus it was intimated that it might be necessary to issue bonds against the enterprise not exceeding $50,000,000, that being the sum that was indicated as the maximum first mortgage bond issue that would be issued against the enterprise, and the earnings were indicated when 500,000 horse-power were installed at $0,200,000 per annum.
5.	The next point to which I direct attention is that when the enterprise began to function it did not take long to exhaust the moneys available from the sale of the $30,000,000 collateral trust bonds, which in fact and in law did not constitute a charge against the physical assets of the enterprise. When the investigations were being carried on by parliament, it became, as I have said, apparent, that further sums would be required, and following the usual course the company applied to the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce for advances secured by bonds, first mortgage bonds, bonds charged against the enterprise. Advances by the banks up to date amount to $6,495,000, and as security for the sums thus advanced the banks hold first mortgage bonds of the undertaking of a face value of $9,742,000.
6.	The next point to which I direct attention is that obviously for reasons that are apparent the banks did not propose to-advance too large sums, because it was not their business to do so, unless they were in some way secured beyond the mere holding of the bonds of the enterprise. The provisions for construction provided for a canal that would be satisfactory for navigation purposes, and would constitute a part of the St. Lawrence waterways as, if and when the St. Lawrence waterways may be completed. In view of the representations made as to what the cost of the canal would be, that is the extra cost involved to make it available for navigation purposes, in the light of what I have said as to its being a connecting link in the St. Lawrence waterways development scheme, an application was made, after the investigation in this house, to the government, to ascertain whether or not it would assist in keeping the enterprise going, and the government undertake, as I shall presently point out, to secure the banks against any loss they might make by advancing to the enterprise further sums of money beyond the sums already indicated. But the government asked that the banks should secure from the

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
enterprise bonds to the extent of 200 per cent of the advances so made, and to date the advances thus made by the banks amount to $7,951,500, and the banks hold as security for such advances, for the purposes of relieving any claim which might arise against the government, bonds of the face value of $15,903,000-that is, first mortgage bonds against the enterprise, it being represented that the total cost of the canal which is to be available for navigation purposes is somewhere between $15,000,000 and $16,000,000, although I personally think that is a somewhat larger figure than the facts warrant for the construction for navigation purposes beyond the construction of a canal for mere power purposes.
7.	Before the house rose last year it will be recalled that on August first, as reported at page 4504 of Hansard, I declared the policy of the government to be as follows:
The government by every means in its power wall endeavour to do the following: (a) secure continuance of the enterprise; (b) secure the rights of those who bona fide have put their money in that enterprise; (c) secure proper control and management; (d) take such other steps as may be necessary when terms and conditions are fixed as will ensure the greatest possible benefit to this dominion as a whole by reason of the undertaking now being declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada.
In the light of that statement and of the position of the undertaking, the government gave the assurances that I have mentioned to the banks, and they-the banks-took security to the extent of approximately two hundred per cent of the sums advanced, the securities being first mortgage bonds of, not the power corporation, but the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company that owns the enterprise.
8.	The next point to which I direct the attention of the house is that in furtherance of the undertaking which I gave to parliament at that time, we first of all secured the continuance of the enterprise. The securing of the rights of those who bona fide had put their money in the enterprise was of course limited and governed by the conditions of the contract under which they had advanced their money. I may add that people in every province advanced money on those second mortgage debentures, or collateral trust bonds as they are called. Subject to the terms of the trust deed, we took every step that could be taken first of all, to see that the terms of the trust deed were observed as to the payment of the half year's interest on the first day of October, 1931-this clause I have just read; and, secondly, that the enterprise was continued as I have just indicated, and that it was controlled and managed in the most efficient way possible. I should say for the information of this house and the country that expenditures to date have been within the estimates made, and the work has progressed up to the point that was expected in view of such expenditures.
9.	The next point I direct attention to is the action taken by the government after the house had risen. On Labour Day I met the representatives of the banks and of the company and of all those interested for the purpose of ascertaining what steps might reasonably be taken for the purpose of advancing the undertaking. Suggestions were made that the enterprise would best be managed by the four existing power companies doing business in the locality in which the Beauharnois Company was functioning. They are the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, Consolidated, the Gatineau Power Company Limited, the Shaw-inigan Power Company and its associated interests, and the Southern Canada Power enterprise. These four power companies are the large enterprises producing hydro-electric energy in the province of Quebec directly affected by this undertaking.
Nothing came of that, and on the 16th day of September, 1931, the premier of Quebec saw me at Ottaw% and with him was a member of his government. They were accompanied by Mr. Geoffrion, K.C., their legal adviser. It was then suggested that the best interests of all would be served if the enterprise were turned over to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, Consolidated, as they had facilities for management, and they would be prepared to do the necessary financing to complete the undertaking. I intimated that that proposal did not commend itself to the government at that time. Within a week Great Britain went off the gold standard, and financing by any body or group of men became impossible. The government continued, however, to take the responsibility I have indicated in connection with the advances that were made in order to enable the work to be continued.
10.	A communication was directed to Mr. Wilson, general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada, who undertook to act as the corresponding medium for the banks that were interested in the undertaking. That letter I will now read because it is important in view of the reply that was made. The letter is dated the 3rd day of October, 1931, and is as follows:
2106	COMMONS
Beauhamois Power-Mr. Bennett
Dear Mr. Wilson:-
Re Beauliarnois Undertaking:
On the 16th of September, the premier of Quebec, the Hon. Honore Mercier and their counsel. Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., interviewed me with respect to the reorganization of the Beauliarnois undertaking.
It is my considered view, as expressed to these gentlemen, that a reorganization of this undertaking, involving a radical change in its directorate and management, is necessary before the Dominion government and parliament can have confidence that the undertaking will be carried to completion in a manner and with results that will adequately safeguard the public interest.
The act respecting the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, which was passed by the parliament of Canada at its last session and which appears as chapter 19 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, approved by Mr. Geoffrion, K.C., on behalf of the province of Quebec, provides, in section 1, for the annulment of the existing orders in council made by the Dominion government and dated March 8, 1921, and June 22, 1929, and also for the annulment of the agreement between the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, and the Dominion government dated June 25, 1929.
I may add that Mr. Geoffrion sent me a note after this letter had been received by Mr. Wilson in which he intimated he thought it was rather too strong to say that he had approved on behalf of the province of Quebec. He was acting for the province when my colleague, the Secretary of State, completed the legislation, and it wiill be recalled that he, Mr. Geoffrion, endorsed his approval on the back of the draft bill, but he regarded that as approval of the form of the bill to accomplish the purpose aimed at rather than as saying that he approved merely on behalf of the province of Quebec, although he was acting as counsel for the province. The letter proceeds:
The second section of that act provides for the grant to the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, of the right to divert the waters of the St. Lawrence river up to but not exceeding 53,072 cubic second feet of water to be used for the development of hydroelectric power "in such manner, upon such terms and conditions and with such limitations and reservations as may be prescribed by order of the governor in council."
The terms of this statute indicate that all relevant negotiations in the future, as in the past, shall take place between the Beauharnois Light. Heat and Power Company, Limited, and the Dominion government;
I should add here that the word "limited" does not appear in the statute. It is incorrect to describe the company as limited, although as a matter of law the liability of the shareholders is limited. The letter continues :

-and it appears to me that as preliminary to a new agreement being negotiated, a reorganization of this company, involving very radical changes in its directorate and management, should forthwith be carried into effect.
I am not unmindful of the fact that the Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, has already issued $30,000,000 of collateral trust sinking fund bonds, which are now held by the public, payment of which is secured by a first fixed and specific charge on all the shares of the capital stock at any time outstanding of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited; and that in the present condition of the financial markets, it may be deemed advisable to avoid any disturbance of this security.
But I understand that the cash advances, which have been made by the banks to enable [DOT] the works to be carried on are secured by a first charge or lien upon the movable and immovable properties of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited; and that provision has already been or can now be made for the creation by this provincial company of such additional bonds as it may be necessary to sell and distribute to the public to provide for the capital expenditures required to utilize for hydro electric power the 55,072 cubic second feet of water presently available.
I would, therefore, suggest that the present board of directors of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, should place their resignations in the hands of those presently interested in the financing of the company and its undertaking; and that those so interested should submit, through you to me, the names of the proposed directors of the new board, indicating what interests they respectively represent.
I would also suggest that arrangements be made forthwith whereby the right to vote a clear majority of the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, be vested in agents or representatives of the three banks who are now financially interested in the undertaking and that these agents or representatives should have the right, by vesting such majority of the shares, to elect and control the personnel of the board of directors for a term of five years, or for such lesser time as may be agreed upon between the representatives of the government of the province of Quebec and of this government.
'The vesting of the right to vote the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, as above suggested, need not prejudicially affect the security for the $30,000,000 of bonds of the Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, now outstanding.
It appears to me possible, if not probable, that such reorganization. as that above suggested; may necessitate the liquidation of the Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, which, subject to outstanding charges thereon, is the holder of the issue capital stock of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited.
It does not appear to me to be incumbent upon the Dominion government, upon the evidence elicited by the parliamentary committee which investigated this undertaking at the last session of parliament, to decide as to the respective legal rights of the holders of the capital stock of the Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited; and, as a matter of fact, the Dominion government has at present no

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
contractual relations with, and, in the future, it is not likely to have any contractual relations with, that company. The shareholders of that corporation should settle and adjust their respective rights and liabilities inter se by mutual agreement or by appropriate legal proceedings. But in any event, all the properties and assets of all subsidiary and associated companies and, or organizations connected with the undertaking of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, should be vested in or held for that company.
In the meantime, however, the Dominion government is prepared to open negotiations with the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, in respect of the parliamentary grant expressed in chapter 19 of the acts of 1931, of the right to divert 53,072 cubic second feet of water of the flow of the river St. Lawrence, and to negotiate with that company as to the terms and conditions, as well as the limitations and reservations, which should be prescribed, under the statute, by order of the governor in council, with respect to such diversion.
It appears to me that the bankers, their associates and clients interested should, forthwith, prepare and present to the government definite proposals with regard to the reorganization of the finances, directorate and management of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, which they will undertake forthwith to carry into effect; and, if these proposals are deemed by the Dominion government to give satisfactory assurance that the undertaking will be carried to a completion efficiently and satisfactorily, then the Dominion government will be prepared to enter at once upon a discussion of the terms and conditions, with such limitations and reservations, as it may be deemed expedient to prescribe by order in council to ensure that Dominion rights and interests, in respect of such diversion of the waters of the river St. Lawrence, shall be properly conserved, and the rights of legitimate investors protected.
If the above proposals are carried into effect, the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, will be placed immediately in a position to complete its negotiations with the Dominion government with respect to the terms of the orders in council which are to be made and promulgated when the act respecting the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company.	Limited, above	mentioned, is
proclaimed and brought into force and effect.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) R. B. Bennett.
Negotiations extending over a period of months were carried on for the purpose of ascertaining just what might be done by those interested in the enterprise to secure its continuance, on the one hand, and that the necessary financial support should foe obtained to enable that continuance to foe carried on, on the other. However, it was not until the month of March this year that the final reply was received from the bankers on behalf of the enterprise. On February 5 intimation was given that the 80,000 shares of stock given to the Sterling Corporation for the purpose of securing such rights as it had on the river
should foe cancelled, and those shares have been turned in for cancellation. The letter dated January 8, reads as follows:
Montreal, January 8, 1932. Dear Mr. Prime Minister:-
Re Beauharnois Undertaking:
As you know, the representatives of the three banks and other persons interested have been giving very full consideration to the suggestions contained in your letter to me of the 3rd October last, and to the various other important points involved in this matter, all of which have been very fully discussed with you on numerous occasions since then, and we feel that it is now appropriate to place before you the considered views and suggestions of the three banks. This letter is written for that purpose, and is concurred in by all three banks.
We believe that this very important undertaking, in which so much money has already been invested, and the success or failure of which will have such an important effect upon the financial and economic condition of the dominion, should be carried forward to a point when the undertaking is producing and delivering power.
We believe that if at all possible those who have in good faith and relying upon grants and approvals made and given by the province of Quebec and the Dominion of Canada purchased securities of the company or lent moneys to it, should have their investments adequately protected.
In connection with the foregoing we have in mind the following salient features:
(a)	The company's auditors report that expenditures upon the project to date have been approximately $39,000,000. Funds for this purpose have been raised as follows:
(i)	proceeds of the sale of collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, and shares of that Corporation represented by share warrants attached to the bonds, $27,000,000.
These collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, of course rank after the first mortgage bonds, mentioned below, of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company.
(ii)	loans from the three banks concerned, secured by first mortgage bonds of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, approximately, $11,900,000.
As you know, the loans from the three banks have been secured by the deposit of first mortgage bonds of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, of a face amount averaging one hundred and seventy-three per cent (173 per cent) of the amount of the loans, and after the loans by the three banks had reached $6,000,000 (the maximum amount of advances which the banks were willing to make) you, from time to time, authorized further advances of approximately $5,900,000 upon the understanding that the Dominion government would protect the banks against any loss.
(b)	We are informed that the balances of money required to place the plant in effective operation so as to meet its contracts, is approximately $13,000,000, of which amount approximately $4,000,000 will be required between now and March 31, 1932.
(c)	During the summer and autumn of 1931 the number of men employed on the site itself
2108	COMMONS
Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
averaged 3,500 and during the current winter season the average number of men employed on the site has been 2,000. In addition, it is estimated that the project gives employment to about 2,000 persons as a result of the extensive purchases of equipment and materials.
It will thus be seen that the banks and the government by cooperating to assist the company in its undertaking have contributed extensively to the relief of unemployment.
(d)	The work has been laid out on a time schedule calculated to bring the power plant into production by October 1, 1932, the date when the two contracts for the sale of substantial and increasing blocks of power to the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario and Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated call for initial deliveries. The reports of the company's officers and engineers show that, so far, the work has been carried out in such a manner that it is now up to schedule as to time, and is also within the estimates of cost made at the outset. It has progressed to such a point that it is reasonable to assume that if carried on without interruption, the power plant can be brought into production by October 1, 1932, and at a cost not exceeding the original estimate for such installation. Should anything intervene to prevent the completion of the work up to this point by October 1, 1932. this would jeopardize these two contracts which are vital to the undertaking. These contracts call for the ultimate delivery of 400,000 h.p. per annum. One of these contracts calls for the ultimate delivery of 250,000 h.p. per annum, and is for a period of forty years, and the other calls for an ultimate delivery of 150,000 h.p. per annum, and is for a period of approximately seventy years.
The banks, having in mind the great importance of the undertaking and the effect which the success or failure of the undertaking will have upon the financial and economic welfare of the Dominion as a whole, and in view of your government's attitude, have felt it incumbent to do their utmost to assist the undertaking financially as they have done, but it is of course obvious that these are loans which the banks should not be asked to carry indefinitely, and that the appropriate method of financing the undertaking is to do so by means of further issues of securities when the financial condition of the markets warrants such steps. It is obvious, however, that no such financing can take place unless and until the orders in council which have become necessary as a result of chapter 19 of the statutes of the last session have been promulgated, and the company is able to go to the investing public with conclusive evidence that its rights in this connection have been satisfactorily and permanently established.
As you have intimated in your letter to me above mentioned, and in your subsequent discussions of the subject with myself and others interested, that the establishment of the terms and conditions of the necessary orders in council hinge to a large extent upon your government being satisfied as to the reorganization of the finances, directorate and management of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, we have considered with you and others interested the various suggestions made in your letter and subsequently, and now have to report as follows:

1.	All the directors of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company (and of the various other companies associated with that company, including Beauharnois Power Corporation. Limited) have placed their written resignations in my hands, and the resignations of three of these, namely, the Hon. Wilfrid L. McDougald, Mr. B. O. Sweezey and Mr. R. A. C. Henry, have been accepted. The acceptance of the resignations of the remaining eight directors has obviously had to be deferred until a new board can be elected, as otherwise the company would be left without a directorate.
2.	There has been submitted to you a list containing the names of nine persons suggested as directors of the company, namely:
Mr. W. A. Black, who is a director of the Bank of Montreal; Mr. C. F. Sise, who is a director of The Royal Trust Company; Mr. W. F. Angus, wffio is a director of The Royal Bank of Canada; Mr. F. B. Common. K.C., who is a partner of Brown, Montgomery & Me-Michael, solicitors of The Royal Bank of Canada; Mr. A. F. White and Mr. Miller Lash, who are directors of The Canadian Bank of Commerce; Mr. J. S. Norris, who is a director of Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated; Sir George Garneau and Mr. Aimc Geoffrion. K.C., who have been selected by the premier of the province of Quebec.
It is, of course, not fair to ask these gentlemen to act unless the company is put in such a position that it will have reasonable prospects of carrying out its financing and its project, which involves primarily its being accorded the necessary approvals by order in council to permit the development of the undertaking and its receiving temporary financial assistance until its permanent financing can be done.
It will be noted that the above list would fill only nine of the eleven seats on the board, the intention being that the other two directors should be persons suggested by your government, or, if the government prefers not to mal*r suggestions in this regard, that these vacancies will be filled only by persons acceptable to the government.
3.	The three banks have given their most serious consideration to the suggestion which you make in your letter to me-
"that arrangements be made forthwith whereby the right to vote a clear majority of the shares of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, Limited, be vested in agents or representatives of the three banks who are now financially interested in the undertaking. and that these agents or representatives should have the right, by voting such majority of the shares, to elect and control the personnel of the board of directors for a term of five years, or such lesser time as may be agreed upon between the representatives of the government of the province of Quebec and this government." but they are extremely reluctant to accept the responsibility of having the voting rights of the shares of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, or a majority of them, vested in representatives of the banks. The banks are of this view for the following reasons:
(a)	That it would be unwise for them to assume the responsibility of having their representatives exercise this voting control;
(b)	That the exercise of such functions by the representatives of the banks would prob-

Beauhamois Power-Mr. Bennett
ably mislead the public into believing that the banks had assumed responsibility for the undertaking of the company and its success or failure, a position in which the banks naturally do not desire to be placed;
(c)	That if the power to remove or to refuse reelection to the directors, or any of them, were vested in the representatives of the three banks, such a power would weaken the directorate's efficiency and dignity, and the existence of such a power in the hands of these representatives would render it difficult to induce the proper type of person to act as a director;	.	,
(d)	That the vesting of such a power in the three representatives of the banks would give too much power and responsibility to these representatives and the banks;
(e)	That if the banks themselves do not require to have their representatives exercise the voting control of the shares, then there would seem to be no reason for asking them to assume that responsibility;
(ft That the same result can be achieved by having Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited (which is now vested with the voting rights of all the shares of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, unless and until the security for the collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, tor which these shares are pledged as security should become enforceable) undertake and agree that for a stipulated period it would vote the shares for the election of a designated list ot directors.
4.	It is therefore suggested-
(a)	That a board of directors of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company consisting of the above mentioned eleven persons should be elected at the outset by Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited (which has the voting rights of all the shares of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company);
(b)	That Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, should give a written undertaking to the government of the Dominion of Canada and to the government of the province of Quebec that unless and until the security for the collateral trust bonds for which the shares of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company are pledged as security shall have become enforceable, the shares in question will be voted (subject to the provisions of (c) below) for the reelection of the designated board; this arrangement to remain in force for a stated number of years;
(c)	That in the case of vacancies occurring in the board, these will be filled by persons appointed by the remaining members of the board, the persons appointed to fill these vacancies to be acceptable to the two governments concerned.
In regard to clauses (b) and (c) above, it is suggested that the term for which this arrangement is to remain in force should terminate on May 1, 1934.
5.	As to the reorganization of the management of the company, we feel that this is a matter which should be left to the new board of directors when they take office,, as this board will be then in a position to study fully the financial, physical and administrative problems of the company and determine what is best in its interests.
6.	In your letter it is suggested that all the properties and assets of all subsidiary and
associated companies and/or organizations connected with the undertaking of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company should be vested in or held for that company.
This suggestion can be carried out as follows:
(a)	By Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, causing to be transferred to Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company (subject to the provisions of the trust deed securing the collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, and all the rights of the trustee thereunder) all the issued shares (except directors' qualifying shares) of Beauharnois Construction Company (which owns all the shares of Marquette Construction Company), Beauharnois Transmission Company and Beauharnois Land Company; and
(b)	By Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, notifying the trustee for the collateral trust bonds of such transfer and acknowledging that the right under the trust deed to receive proxies in respect of the shares of such subsidiaries as are pledged to the trustee is vested in Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company instead of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited.
In this manner the properties and assets of the subsidiaries will be held for Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company as the sole shareholder of those subsidiaries (aside from directors' qualifying shares), subject to the rights of the trustee for the collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited.
This method would carry out the second alternative proposed in your suggestion. This second alternative is preferable to the first alternative for the following among other reasons:
(i)	It is more expeditious, less cumbersome and less expensive than the first alternative;
(ii)	If the physical assets of the subsidiaries were themselves transferred to Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, they would be subject to the limitations created by the trust deed securing the collateral trust bonds of Beauharnois Power Comporation, Limited, which restrict the amount of bonds and similar securities which may be issued secured upon the assets of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, and the purposes for which such bonds and similar securities may be issued, and places other restrictions upon such issue, whereas no restrictions are placed upon the issue of bonds and similar securities of the other subsidiaries. This is important, because such other subsidiaries will doubtless require to issue bonds and similar securities in order to carry out their respective undertakings; and
(iji) Some at least of these other subsidiaries have assets which are not required for or directly connected with the undertaking of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. For example, some of these subsidiaries have lands acquired with a view to furnishing factory sites, housing developments, etc. It is therefore appropriate and advisable that these assets should be kept separate from the assets of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company.
7. One of the first duties of the new board when elected would be to prepare a plan for the future financing of the company and any reorganization which that might involve. We would earnestly hope that this would not involve the liquidation of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, as we feel that such a

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
step would seriously prejudice or embarrass the future financing of the undertaking and it might cause injury and injustice to a wide list of shareholders and others who in good faith have invested their money in the securities of Beauharnois Power Corporation, Limited, relying upon the rights which that company's subsidiaries had acquired.
We hope that the foregoing suggestions will prove acceptable to the Dominion government, and that negotiations may now be commenced and brought to a speedy termination with respect to the terms of the orders in council which are to be promulgated when the Dominion statute respecting Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company is brought into effect.
It is needless for me to add that the representatives of the three banks (Bank of Montreal, The Royal Bank of Canada and The Canadian Bank of Commerce) are ready at all times to further those negotiations and to discuss with you in detail any of the suggestions made above.
Yours faithfully,
M. W. Wilson.
The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, P.C.. Iv.C., Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Canada.
There was also the letter dated February 5, in which it was indicated, as I have already stated, that the 80,000 shares issued to the Sterling Corporation had been turned in for cancellation in accordance with the demands made by the government. Negotiations were carried on with the banks and their representatives, legal and otherwise, and in the end, as this house knows, an order in council was passed confirming, by a title superior to that which had theretofore prevailed, the grant of the 53,000 odd second feet of the river, and the provisions, conditions and reservations under which that grant is made appear in the order in council tabled in this house some few days ago. The proclamation duly issued, the statute became operative and the order in council is, as I have said, predicated upon that authority.
11.	I next direct attention to the fact that on existing economic conditions which need not here be further alluded to than mentioned, the difficulties of financing were very great, that is the difficulties of selling first mortgage securities at the time, but in view of the position in which the undertaking was, we did in the manner indicated ensure its continuance up to the present time. Among the suggestions which were made was one that they might be able to secure assistance from the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, and negotiations, I believe, were carried on in that sense as well as with one or other or all of the power companies I have mentioned. April 1, being the half-year in-
terest day, arrived and the company was without funds with which to pay its interest on the second mortgage collateral trust bonds. The government did not feel warranted in making any provision for the payment of interest on these securities in view of the terms of the trust deed which constituted the contract between the debenture holders, or the holders of the second mortgage collateral trust bonds and the issuing company, namely, the Beauharnois Power Corporation, for it will be recalled by the house, as I read from the document, provision is made that out of the proceeds derived from the sale of these collateral trust bonds, interest was to be provided up to the first day of October last and no provision was made for any date beyond that. We therefore felt under no responsibility in that regard, for it will be observed that nothing was said in the house or elsewhere at any time indicating that the government would place or would ask parliament to place the debenture holders or, as they are called, the holders of the collateral trust bonds, in any better position than they had placed themselves by the contract they had made when the securities were issued.
12.	I next direct attention to the fact that during the progress of the negotiations and discussions and, in fact, recently the exact terms of the contract between the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, and the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, that is the parent company, first became known in detail to the government. It will be recalled that at the investigation the contract was referred to, but its exact terms did not seem to be a matter of very great importance beyond the fact that a given quantity of power was to be delivered, rising with the lapse of time to a maximum, and the price fixed for it was to be uniform with the price paid by other purchasers of power from the enterprise. I have, however, since obtained a copy of the contract and paragraph 10 becomes one of very great importance. Paragraph 10, which will be found commencing at page 20 of the typewritten contract, reads as follows:
Territorial, (a) It is agreed that during the term of this contract the company will not, without the written consent of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, sell or distribute electrical power or energy, either directly or indirectly, within the territory which is or may be served directly or indirectly by the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, which territory is understood for purposes of this agreement to be limited to the island of Montreal and such territory as may lie within a radius of thirty miles from Place d'Armes square, in the city of Montreal, provided the territory so defined shall not at any time be deemed to include any part of the counties of Beauharnois, Huntingdon and Chateauguay, and that portion of the

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
counties of Vereheres and Richelieu fronting on the St. Lawrence river to a depth of five miles from the said river; and it is further agreed that the Montreal Light, Heat and Power will not, either directly or indirectly, sell or distribute any electric power or energy in the said three counties of Beauharnois, Huntingdon and Chateauguay.
(b) It is also agreed that each of the parties hereto will assist the other in procuring the necessary right of way for the passage of through-going transmission lines across the territories of each of them as hereinabove defined and will mutually facilitate the passage of such transmission line or lines.
The exclusive right to sell power within a radius of thirty miles from Place d'Armes square, that is a total width of sixty miles, is by this company conceded to the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, which company in turn concedes to the Beauharnois enterprise the right to sell power within the three counties of Beauharnois, Huntingdon and Chateauguay, and on the river St. Lawrence for a depth of five miles in the counties of Ver-cheres and Richelieu. That of course has a distinct bearing upon the attitude of other power enterprises towards interesting themselves in this undertaking.

13.	The next question to which attention should be directed is that which affects the rights of the $30,000,000 collateral trust bondholders. If the members of the house are interested, I shall give them the page of the trust deed on which the provisions in that regard will be found. Article 19, page 51, provides for meetings of bondholders and the provisions with respect to default being made by the enterprise in payment of its interest. There is the usual acceleration clause by which the whole $30,000,000 can be declared to become due, and thereafter follow the usual provisions in trust deeds for the remedies that accrue in case of default. They will be found in article 7, commencing at page 30 of the trust,deed. Shortly, after providing for the acceleration of principal and interest whereby the whole $30,000,000, with interest, may be declared to be presently due, it provides for entry into possession and restoration upon removal of default-that is not of importance- the sale by the trustees of the shares and the method by which those who desire to acquire them may use their bonds for the purpose of discharging the purchase price. There is a provision for the appointment of a receiver
or receiver manager by the trust company and the other usual provisions in that regard. I shall not trouble the house by reading them, but I think it is important they should be borne in mind.
The position at the moment, if I might direct the attention of the house to the matter, is that there has been default in the payment of interest due on April 1 to the holders of the $30,000,000 6 per cent collateral trust bonds of the enterprise; that that default must continue for a period of ninety days, which would be the months of May, June and July, to enable the holders of those securities to avail themselves of the provisions of the trust deed whereby they may exercise their rights of foreclosure, that is call for the payment of the whole sum, sell the shares and other securities that they hold for their bonds, and become practically, to all intents and purposes, the owners of the enterprise subject to the first mortgage bonds. That, I think the house will observe, is all they stipulated for when they made their advances of money on the security of the bonds, but to-day the parent company whose shares are their security has, subject to the observance of the terms and conditions of the order in council, a title to the water, which title it did not have before the investigation and which arises by reason of the fact that the 53,000 cubic second feet have been granted to them on the terms and conditions mentioned in the order in council under an act of the parliament of Canada which was assented to last year and declared effective by proclamation, I think on March 1 last.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Will the bondholders be represented on the new directorate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We have not got that
far yet; I was just going to mention that. What action the holders of the $30,000,000 of the collateral trust bonds now in default may take is a matter for them to determine. There is a provision whereby the company may by extraordinary resolution appoint a committee in the meantime, which right I understand has been exercised; but the debenture holders themselves under the provisions of this trust deed may meet together and have a regular meeting for the purpose of determining what action they desire to take with respect to their enterprise, and it rests with them either by proceedings under the trust deed itself in the manner therein prescribed, or by arrangement, whichever is thought the more desirable, to determine what action they shall take.

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
In answer to the hon. member for Antigon-ish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) may I point out to him that subject to the first mortgage bonds the debenture holders may, if they so desire, by appropriate proceedings become the owner of every share of stock of the parent enterprise to which I first referred, namely, the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. The question of being represented on the board is not the question at the moment for they themselves may become the proprietors of an enterprise subject to the bond issue which I have mentioned.
14.	It has been suggested that the government should guarantee the bonds of the enterprise and that other proceedings of various kinds should be taken. But we have now discharged our duty to these debenture holders, as they are called, the holders of these second mortgage collateral trust bonds of the enterprise. We have not only observed in detail and scrupulously the obligations which as I indicated to this house we regarded it as our duty to undertake, namely, (a) securing the continuance of the enterprise and (b) securing the rights of those who bona fide put their money into the enterprise, but I fancy that we have done that more scrupulously than they ever expected that it would be done, for it will be observed that of the total par value of these $30,000,000 bonds a little more than half, certainly not seventy per cent, became available for the enterprise, and two years' interest, $3,600,000 was paid back to them out of their own money. In addition it will be observed that the moneys paid to the syndicate-
Mr. STEWART (Edmonton) The $3,600,000 interest that is provided for in the agreement, and nothing beyond that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Yes, the S3,600,000 provided for in the agreement.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The amount set aside for interest was specifically mentioned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I want to make that
quite clear. Paragraph 2 (a) of Article nine provides for interest up to the first day of October, 1931. That paragraph reads as follows:
For the payment from time to time of the instalments of interest falling due in respect of the bonds up to and including the interest payable on the first day of October, 1931 (October 1, 1931).
That is the limit as to date. In other words, the payment out of their own money of the interest for the two years.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: And not beyond in the construction period?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: No, not during the construction period, for in the prospectus upon which the securities were sold it is apparent that it was never expected that the work would be completed for the purpose of supplying either in partial form the contracts entered into or the whole until at least October, 1932-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is why I asked the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I want to make clear that there is no provision in the documents that we have seen, and they tell us that these are the only relevant documents for interest after the first day of October, 1931.
Therefore we have secured during the interim control and management and it is so satisfactory, the engineers certify, that their expectations both as to the amount of work that would be done by a given date as well as the cost of it have been more than met, and we have taken such other steps as we think a government might reasonably be expected to take, and perhaps many in this house will think perhaps more than we might reasonably be expected to take, to ensure that they have not only the continuance of their enterprise but their water rights, available for the parent company on the security of the shares of which the advances were made, and to-day they are in a better legal position than they were prior to the date of the passing of the statute of last year and the order in council based thereon.
15.	I have further heard it suggested that the language used by me last year contemplated that we were going to guarantee the payment of interest on these second mortgage securities. That is the reason that I have taken the trouble to read the exact words as they appear in Hansard as used in the House of Commons. Further, I think the answer is more complete when I state this, that the securities themselves, instead of rising in value, have decreased in value, which indicates at once the understanding that was placed by the public upon what we undertook to do and have done. In no event was it ever suggested that we should do more than protect them to the extent to which they protected themselves; and to the extent to which they have protected themselves, we have protected them. In addition to that we have gone further and secured for them, through the parent company as I have said, water rights that are beyond any possible chance of being attacked.
16.	As to the future, that is a matter, as the house will see, as to which the second

Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
mortgage debenture holders, or the collateral trust bond holders, whichever term you desire to use, must in the very nature of things, take such steps as they think appropriate for the purpose of exercising the rights that are created and granted to them under the terms of the trust deed to which I have referred. We have indicated, as I said at the very threshold of my observations, that as this project was by common consent, alike by the late administration and by this, treated as an undertaking that was a link in the St. Lawrence waterway and that the canal should be a canal that would be available to navigation if as and when that' undertaking is proceeded with-we have indicated our willingness to take a very reasonable view of the situation, that is, as to the extra cost involved in constructing a canal for navigation, and if a plan of reorganization is arrived at the government will consider sympathetically, at least, any proposal that may be made involving the acquisition by the government of first mortgage securities to the extent to which the cost might represent the extra cost of the canal for navigation as distinguished from power purposes. But that in any event would not involve us in any payment that would not be repaid under the terms of the bonds themselves. In other words, it might be advisable and in the public interest that by the acquisition of first mortgage bonds funds may be provided in the same way as from any purchaser, for the purpose of enabling them to carry forward the undertaking to which they are now committed and in which they have placed their money to the extent I have indicated from the documents I have read.
17.	I think, Mr. Speaker, that that covers the position so far as I can place it before the house at this moment. I think it answers the questions that have been asked by the various members of the house during the last few weeks, and I offer my apologies, sir, for having trespassed so long on the time of the house, but there was no method which I knew of by which the matter could be clearly placed before the house other than by the reading of the documents which refer to the undertaking and its present position.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Might I ask whether the government concedes the claims of the province of Quebec with regard to the water powers or whether the government would consider placing before the supreme court a stated case as to the ownership and jurisdiction of water powers on the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I may say in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the question has already been submitted 41761-133
to the supreme court. The answers are unsatisfactory; I think that is a fair way to put it. But having regard to the relation of this enterprise to navigation, and to its being a unit in the development of the St. Lawrence waterway, I see no reason why at this particular moment that should be done. It is not improbable that some day the question will be determined on a concrete case, but references by questions have always been found unsatisfactory. The privy council has itself indicated that it very greatly preferred that such should not be done, that it did not feel itself bound by the answers when a concrete case did arise, and further that the opinion thus given in answer to questions was not better than that of the law officers of the crown. For these reasons I am greatly disposed always to avoid references on abstract questions when concrete cases may ultimately determine the issue.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Has the Prime Minister any objection to placing on Hansard the agreement between the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company and the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company-the whole agreement? The Prime Minister has read an extract from it, and it is a very important document.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT

If the house desires I
will hand the agreement to Hansard, so that not only paragraph 10 but the whole of the contract may be printed. Obviously however that could be done only with the consent of the house, because it is not part of the particular matter to which I referred. If it is desired however I shall be very glad to do so. It might be put into votes and proceedings-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That would be all right.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is satisfactory.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: It seems to me that this is not an abstract question in the sense it was a few years ago, when the first presentation was made. To-day it is a very concrete question, and as such it is in an altogether different position.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
Prime Minister if re-organization has yet taken place and if the nine gentlemen mentioned by Mr. Wilson, as directors, have been appointed, or if the government has appointed the two they are to appoint?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend
from Antigonish-Guysborough follows me

2114	COMMONS
Beauharnois Power-Mr. Bennett
when I say that it is now no longer the prerogative of the power corporation to appoint directors, for the debenture holders- that is, the collateral trust bond holders, as they are mentioned in the trust deed-can in the ninety days now avail themselves of their rights. subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Am I going too far in asking whether or not there is a very great distinction between the situation at this time and the situation at the time when the former questions were submitted to the supreme court?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
gentleman is undoubtedly correct in saying there is a difference, but the difference is not such as would be reflected in any questions which might be framed. I endeavoured to make clear that the mere framing of questions, however carefully and intelligently it may be done, is fraught with no final result, or brings about no final determination, for the reasons given by the privy council itself. They are no better than an opinion of the law officers of the crown. But it is competent for litigation to be instituted and the matter determined in the light of evidence submitted.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: In the event of the second mortgage bondholders taking action, as they are entitled to do, on the date fixed, would there be priority for all the issue of the first mortgage bonds, or only such as are hypothecated for purposes of carrying on the enterprise.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF POSITION OF UNDERTAKING AND POLICY OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: That is very difficult for me to answer, as a matter of law, without going into the matter with some care. Offhand I would say the courts would determine that the advances made would be the determining factor.
