The Budget-Mr. Mullins

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Hon. E. N. Rhodes (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston, and the proposed amendment to the amendment of Mr. Gardiner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house adjourned on Thursday night I was endeavouring to place on Hansard some of the reasons for the low cost of farm commodities, a subject referred to foy the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophail) and the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). They spoke of the great difficulties affecting agriculture, but they offered no explanation for its 'being in its present shape. I have endeavoured to satisfy myself why the primary products of the farms are selling at such low prices to-day. Take our importations of canned meats. These importations, I may tell my critics opposite, are larger than I expected to find them. From the Argentine, a favoured country with whom we have a treaty made by 'hon. gentlemen opposite, we imported in 1930 canned meats to the extent of 7,087,820 pounds, from all countries a total of 8,758,250 pounds; in 1931 our total importations amounted to 5,992,336 pounds. All critics thrive during a depression; that is the time they get their work in. I wonder if our critic from Southeast Grey endeavoured to find out why our farm products were affected to that extent? We are told the price of hogs is low,-four cents a pound. I admit it, but there is a reason for this low price. As I told the house before it adjourned on Thursday night, a corporation in the city of Toronto imported two carloads of hams on July 28 and 29, 1931, from the United States. They brought them in under a duty of five cents a pound, expecting to get away with that duty, but the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) put on a dumping duty, and that firm did not attempt any further importations. But those two carloads broke the market in Toronto by one-half for the Canadian raised product, which is far superior to that imported from the United States. If I were at liberty to tell how those American hogs are raised and fed as compared with the Canadian hogs, I think it would surprise this house, and our people 41761-1331
would not buy the imparted article. I see my friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) laughing.
I wonder that even he, a low tariff man, would permit American hams to come in and break the 'bacon market for our farmers. That is why the price of hogs went down a cent a pound. In 1931 we also imported from the United States 8,242,059 pounds of barrelled pork in brine. I want hon. members to get these figures, particularly the hon. member for South Huron. They might have been useful to him when 'he was telling the house how he intended to help agriculture, although he tries to block us on this side of the house when we are doing everything humanly possible to aid that great basic industry agriculture to get out of the hole. Through the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite that staggering quantity of pork in brine was brought into this country under a low duty. Some of it is even coming in free. It is brought in to ship stores in bond, and is then taken out beyond the three mile limit where it is used by our fishermen. If I had my way I would not permit them to eat that pork because I know 'how the hogs are raised and fed in the United States. I would prefer to have them supplied with the Canadian fed product. The Americans are getting the benefit of that business. Why won't you protect the Canadian grown product and so protect the Canadian farmer? Before I get out of the Marquette seat I will have protection for the farmer's primary products- protection is abused so much by our critics opposite. I want the Minister of Inland Revenue to listen to this, because I desire 'him to apply the dumping duty and save the situation in Canada. For the manufacture of cottonseed meal and refined cottonseed oil we are bringing into Canada from the United States 180,169 hundredweight of crude cottonseed oil; peanut oil and refining oil for edible purposes we imported to the extent of 337,163 hundredweight. That product was brought in to compete with the fine lard of this country, the best shortening you can have. These figures have been furnished by the Bureau of Statistics and they must be correct. The imports of cottonseed oil amounted to 8,218,214 pounds and of other vegetable oils, 68,885,823 pounds. The house should consider these figures; this material is coming into this country to compete with our hog raising industry. I see hon. members laughing, but it is nothing to laugh about. They are willing, in the agriculture committee, to talk their heads off about wheat, but the country would be better off if more time was spent in the
The Budget-Mr. Mullins

discussion of the hog raising industry. Hon. members talk nothing but wheat and then wail and cry that this government is to blame for present day conditions in t'he live stock industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware
that last session the agriculture committee spent nearly all its time talking about hogs?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What has been done this last two weeks? Wheat has been the only matter under discussion. There has been some talk about the whiskers on wheat, but nothing about hogs. The committee has been spending its time discussing durum and other varieties of wheat, why does it not discuss pure bred cattle and help conditions in Canada? This country cannot exist without live stock. A farm does not look like a farm unless there are some live stock. When I go on a farm and see a lot of machinery scattered all over, it does not look like a farm to me. As I said some years ago, a sowless and chickenless farm is not the proper type of farm for this country; this country needs mixed farming. The figures which I have quoted give the true reasons why this industry has been driven into the ground by low prices. I have heard the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) speak on the tariff. The following was said a short time ago by the hon. member for Provencher:
If the hon. members for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), Souris (Mr. Willis), Selkirk (Mr. Stitt), Portage ia Prairie (Mr. Burns), Dauphin (Mr. Bowman), Nelson (Mr. Stitt), Springfield (Mr. Hay), and Brandon (Mr. Beaubier) had told their electors that if the present Prime Minister was returned to power lie would increase the tariff. I do not believe they would be here to-day. They know that very well, and they know that they told the electors that the Conservative party was not a high tariff party. Can they go back to their electors to-day and tell them that? If they do they will be misleading those who put them in office.
The Conservative party was never a high-tariff party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh if they wish, but that is the fact. For a considerable period I lived next door to the son of that great man, Sir John A. Macdonald; I sat in the provincial houses with him and I have visited him in his home. I have talked over that great national policy of his illustrious father, and he told me that it was never his father's intention that that policy should be based on high tariff principles to injure the consumer. That is not

the policy of the right hon. gentleman now leading this government; it is his intention that no oppression shall be placed upon the consumer. Hon. members should not forget that advertisement which appeared in the Journal the other day. Hon. members opposite put the duty on agricultural implements down until it had reached six per cent, but all the time the price of machinery was climbing in price until it finally reached a prohibitive figure. A large manufacturing company in Toronto has reduced the price of machinery by ten per cent and has allowed a reduction of the same amount on all debts due to the company. That means that to-day a binder can be purchased for $28 less than it could have been purchased during the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite. How can hon. gentlemen answer that fact? There is a tariff of 25 per cent on agricultural implements, but the price is coming down. I can remember in 1891 when the duty on agricultural machinery was 35 per cent, a binder could be purchased for $150; under the late administration the duty was reduced to six per cent but the price of a binder had gone up to $281. How can hon. members explain that to the electors? Put the tariff up just as long as the price of the machinery comes down. I want some degree of protection to save this great agricultural industry for the people of Marquette. I met the president of the Massey-Harris Company in front of this building and told him that he never would be able to sell machinery in western Canada with the present low price of wheat. The farmer needs new machinery. I helped a friend of mine for half a day to repair an old mower. There was a broken cog in one of the wheels and we were trying to get the machine together. The price of machinery must be lowered or the western farmer will be put out of business.
This is an answer to the free trade critics on the other side. Free trade is not possible in this country, when all countries have protection. I remember some years ago when I was in England walking around the tower of London, I wondered why so many men were loitering around the tower. I asked one man and he told me he was out of work. He said he had worked for forty years for one company without losing a day's work, but that they had put up two poles, one bearing a large loaf and the other a small loaf of bread and he was asked to vote for the large loaf. He told me that his present condition made it impossible to buy the large loaf and that if he had realized what he was doing, he would have voted so that he would have had sufficient money to buy the small

The Budget-Mr. Mullins
loaf. At that time he was receiving only one day's work per week, and that was the result he obtained from free trade. Germany entered the British market and undersold the home product, and this man was put out of work. We cannot have free trade with protection all around us.
I am sorry the hon. member for Southeast Grey is not in her place. I do not know why she always leaves the chamber when I speak. It may be because I am not very interesting or because of my grey hairs. I shall not discuss the tariff any longer, but will go on to another matter. I find in this morning's Journal a severe criticism of the project which has been the hope of western Canada and which was to assist in the moving of our products. I am referring now to the Hudson Bay railway. The people of western Canada have been living in hopes of being able to ship their produce out of that country by some means or other, and if it is not to be by way of Hudson bay, then let us deepen the St. Lawrence waterway, so that we may be enabled to ship our products out; because no man can farm and pay present freight rates. This article on Hudson bay is just another one of the Journal's pipe dreams. It published a good many articles of the same kind when I was here in 1926; it did not give a tinker's curse for Mullins or anybody else who had anything to do with the Hudson Bay railway. I ask hon. members to read for themselves the statements made in that article with regard to navigation in that great channel. That channel is navigable; it can be made navigable, and I hope to live to see the day when liners will be going out of there in large numbers.
Now I come to the question of unemployment. This country is fdled with the unemployed and the great question is-What shall we do with them? There is just one answer: they must go back to the land. They must be taught that tilling the soil is not a disgrace. They left the land a few years ago and crowded into the cities, which to-day are filled with unemployed who will do any kind of menial work. A good many men want to be doctors, preachers and lawyers, and they will do anything so as to escape the drudgery of the farm. These men must be turned back to the land. They must become producers; they must make homes on the prairies. I want to see men happy and comfortable so that they will be contented citizens.
There is another thing I want to mention with reference to the unemployed who appeared on parliament hill a few weeks ago. On that occasion I happened to walk down
from the building and it struck me forcibly, as I looked at the sidewalks, to see it littered with cigarette butts. I wondered what the idea was. Before I leave this House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, I am going to bring in a resolution to prohibit the news stands from selling cigarettes to minors. Just think of what you see in the streets of the cities today. A little girl of fifteen driving a motor car, with a cigarette stuck between her fingers. A short time ago I was driving my daughter's car in Toronto when one of these little girls nearly smashed into me, and all I could see was her nose above the wheel and a big cigarette in her fingers. These girls will never make mothers. I leave it to any medical man in this house to say whether I am right or not. I want to read into Hansard a statement that appeared in the Toronto Star some time ago, bearing on this subject, because it will show what sort of women these girls will make when they grow to womanhood. Youngsters of twelve and fourteen years will go up to news stands and buy cigarettes, in one of these cheap cigar places. A well-regulated cigar store will not sell cigarettes to minors. What are our provincial governments doing? A few days ago I saw a gentleman from the city of Ottawa taking four delinquent boys to Toronto. When he got off this side of Toronto to go to the home, one of the little chaps pulled a cigarette out of his pocket and lit it behind the gentleman's back. It was easy to see where that boy would land in later life. It is these boys and girls that I want to save. In the Toronto Star on March 19, there appeared the following:
Surely it cannot be that in the face of such evidence as that furnished by Mayo Brothers, of the Rochester Clinic, of Dr. Kellogg of the Kellogg Institute, Dr. D. H. Kress, neurologist, Washington sanatorium hospital, and countless others, the publishers of The Star would want to see the girls and women of Canada become addicted to the cigarette. Dr. Kress has said that if young women take up this habit, there will be a landslide in physical and moral degeneracy.
At a medical association conference in Chicago in 1928, a woman doctor of Detroit who had made a study of this phase of the cigarette habit, extending over a period of twenty years, reported that 62 infants out of every 100, born to cigarette smoking mothers never lived beyond the second year. A prominent physician in Washington, D.C., stated that of 5.000 maternity cases coming under his observation not one mother was able to nurse her baby, if she smoked cigarettes.
They put a leech on the arm of one cigarette smoking woman and the leech died from nicotine drawn from her system. It is to be regretted that such an example should be set the rising generation.
The Budget-Mr. Young

I am not opposed to smoking; I find no fault with a man of mature age who does so. Indeed, there is nothing I like better than to see a man in front of a fireplace, lighting his pipe; but I detest looking at a woman smoking cigarettes. The first woman I ever saw smoking a cigarette was in the city of Rome, Italy. When I saw her light one of these things I thought what a remarkable thing it was. Now you can see scarcely a woman who does not smoke. They nearly all have the pernicious habit in cities.
My time is about up, but I will say this in conclusion. I want the old days back; I do not want present day conditions. Present day conditions will not make Canada what we all want to see this country become. I say: What are you doing? Are you changing? Yes; you have the specialist now. Well, I want the old family doctor back. I do not want the specialist that looks me over first to see how much I have and then takes everything off my back. You can tax a lawyer- and, God help them, we have lots of them here-but you cannot tax one of these specialists. He takes your statement, figures how much you can stand, and then prescribes for you accordingly. Again, I want to see the old storekeeper back in the towns, not the department stores, I want to have the old cattle buyer back in the field-the man who comes to the farmer and says, "How much do you want for these cattle?" And the farmer, with some initiative of his own, states his price and does his own business right there. Give me 'back the old timers, the conditions we had in the early days, and do away with your new corporations, wheat pools and everything else, that has not competent management.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
it does not suit their convenience might have a disastrous effect on their business. If our rubber manufacturers, for instance, find it profitable to buy their raw rubber in New York instead of in Malay where it is produced, it must be because it pays them to do so, and if at the coming Imperial conference tariffs should be so arranged as to force those manufacturers to buy their raw material in the country of origin and bring it directly to Canada through our own ports, it might conceivably have the effect of adding so substantially to the cost of that raw rubber that our manufacturers would not be able to compete in the world's markets.
We also hear rumours of plans being made to establish complementary industries within the empire-that is to say, assigning different industries to different parts of the empire; saying to Canada, for instance, you are better suited to the production of such and such products, so you confine yourself to them; saying to Australia, you are better suited to producing these products, so you confine yourself to them; and so on. I do not think that any government, even this one, would be foolish enough to adopt such a policy as that, and hence I shall not waste any time on it.
But there is one matter that is of vital concern to us all, and that is those sections of our Customs Act which give the minister power to fix values for duty purposes, and thereby to raise the tariff at will. I refer to sections 35 to 43 inclusive, of the Customs Act and to the dumping clause in the customs tariff. So long as those sections remain on our statute books any agreement that may be entered into at the conference will not be worth the paper it is written on. It will be absolutely worthless. If at this conference, with these sections still on the statute books, our government should make an agreement with the governments of other parts of the empire to admit their goods into this country under certain conditions, and if the exporters in those countries were then to ship their goods to Canada thinking that they would enter this country under the terms of that agreement, the minister under the clauses I have mentioned could shut out those goods at will. The sections to which I refer should be repealed before this parliament prorogues. Otherwise it is the duty of the Prime Minister at the opening of the conference to say to the representatives of the different governments assembled: "Gentlemen, we are here if possible to make trade arrangements with you, but before engaging upon that task I

must warn you that we have certain provisions on our statute books that will enable us at will to raise the duty against your goods and shut them out by that means in spite of any agreement we may reach at this conference." If the delegates from Great Britain and other parts of the empire are wise, they will refuse absolutely to make any agreements with us so long as those provisions are on the statute books. But I want to urge upon the minister the necessity of repealing these clauses before going into the conference, or at least of assuring the delegates from other parts of the empire that they will not be applied against them.
The Prime Minister, in a previous debate this session, made a remark that is rather disturbing. He said that he hoped that at the conference they would be able to discover some means of stabilizing the exchange values of the currencies of the empire. What does that mean? To stabilize the exchange values of the currencies of the empire simply means that we will agree to redeem each other's currencies at certain fixed values. If we should agree to purchase British pounds at the rate of four Canadian dollars to the pound and Britain agreed to purchase Canadian dollars at the price of four to. the British pound, and then the Canadian dollar should go below that value, Britain would be in a position of having to redeem our dollars for more than they were worth. The value of a country's currencies depends very largely upon certain factors that are under the control of the government of that country, and not under any outside control. If the various governments were to agree on certain exchange values for their respective currencies, and if one of those countries should see fit to act in such a way that its currency becomes worthless, how can we expect other parts of the empire to redeem that currency at the price agreed upon? We have in this house some who .would depreciate our own currency to half its present value. Suppose that at this conference we agree with Great Britain to -buy her pounds at four Canadian dollars to the pound, and she agrees to buy our dollars at four to the pound, and then that the men having these ideas as to currency get into power and depreciate our dollars to one-half its present value. Under those circumstances could we expect the British government to live up to its agreement and redeem our currency at the figure agreed upon? The thing is absurd. Backing each other's notes is poor policy for nations, as it is for individuals. Our delegates going into that conference could

The Budget-Mr. Young
not do better than to memorize and keep ever in their minds the words of Edmund Burke:
In politics it not infrequently happens that the magnanimous course is the profitable course. Great empires and little minds go ill together.
I would like to say a few words in regard to the subamendment. It reads in part as follows:
Therefore, be it resolved, that in the opinion of this house, as a first step towards general economic reconstruction, our financial system should be nationalized, and provision be made to issue immediately sufficient money to bring the value of the dollar as speedily as possible to that point at which the major portion of our debts were incurred during the war; stabilize the dollar at this point internally and thereafter manage credit and currency issue to secure and maintain a stable price level within Canada.
The object of the subamendment seems to be to stabilize the price level. In my opinion the trouble with the price level is not that it is not stable, but that it is not level. The difficulty is not the price level but the inequalities within the price level. The existence of society, the very existence of the human race itself on the earth to-day, depends upon the division of labour and the exchange of goods. The world could not sustain her present population by any other means. It is only by the division of labour and the exchange of goods that it is possible for the world to produce enough of the necessities of life to support its present papulation. But the exchange must be equitable. That is to say, making due allowances for differences in skill and differences in the degree of application with which different men work, the exchange should be on an equal basis, that one man's labour is equal to that of another. One day of your labour ought to be as valuable as one day of my labour, and the product of your day's labour should exchange for the product of my day's labour. But that condition does not prevail. We all know, we see on every hand, men drawing big wages for rendering very little service. We also see men rendering valuable service and receiving very small wages. These are inequalities that must foe ironed out. It is not so much the price level as the inequalities within it.
We have been told in this debate that the price of primary products to-day is just fifty per cent of what it was two years ago and that the price of manufactured goods i3 eighty-five per cent of what it was two years ago. If you adjust the price level, raise the whole level as my friends to my left would, by inflating the currency, what would happen? You would bring back the price of primary
products to one hundred per cent of what it was two years ago, and at the same time you would raise the price of manufactured goods to one hundred and seventy per cent of what it was two years ago. Can you solve the farmers' problem in that way? As at what date, I ask you, would you stabilize the price level? My friend says that he would stabilize it at the price goods were when most of our debts were incurred. I make this challenge; Name any date you like in this century, in the last century or in any other century, and say that you would stabilize the price level as of that date; I will prove to you that the price level at that date was not equitable, that prices within the level were not fair and just to all. This proposal to correct things by raising or lowering the whole price level will never iron out those inequalities. What is the trouble in Canada to-day? Is it not this: We produce a certain limited variety of commodities, and produce them in vast quantities-more than we can use ourselves. We have a surplus of those commodities which we must sell abroad. When the producers of such commodities can sell their goods abroad they receive in exchange purchasing power, which goes into circulation in Canada and creates employment in all other forms of industry. At the present time our primary producers, those of us who produce goods for export, find they cannot sell their exportable surplus. They have no purchasing power with which to buy other goods in Canada. They have to reduce their staffs. Those from whom they are in the habit of buying have to reduce staffs, bringing about the unemployment and the trouble we are having to-day.
The subamendment proposes to remedy this condition by some change in our financial system, by some change in our currency system, or some change in our banking system. I ask hon. members this question:	Why can
we not sell our wheat? The Minister of Trade and Commerce explained the reason the other night, namely that European governments have decided not to admit it to their countries. The same applies to our newsprint, our lumber and practically everything we have to sell. I ask my hon. friend from Acadia this question: What change will you make in our banking system; what change will you make in our credit system; what change will you make in our currency system that will persuade the people of Europe to buy our wheat, if their governments will not allow them to import it? What change will you make in our banking system;
The Budget-Mr. Young

what change will you make in our credit system; what change will you make in our currency system, that will give us a better price for our wheat, if our own government will not allow us to bring that price into the country when we get it?
I think I understand the argument concerning inflation. They say the farmer to-day is loaded with a vast burden of debt which he incurred during a period of inflation and which he now has to liquidate during a period of deflation. They say when he borrowed $2,000 a few years ago he was borrowing the equivalent of a thousand bushels of wheat. To-day he has to pay it back with the equivalent of three thousand bushels of wheat. That is true. A real difficulty arises there. But I ask hon. members this question: Who hold the mortgages on the farms of this country? Most of them are held by the great life insurance companies, and when loaning money on mortgage most of those life insurance companies insist that the mortgagor take out a life insurance policy for an amount somewhat larger than the face of the mortgage. That has had the double advantage of increasing the life insurance business and improving the security of the loan.
Let us consider the case of the farmer who mortgaged his farm for say $2,000 during the period of inflation, and took out a life insurance policy for $3,000 at the same time. If the proposals in the subamendment were carried out and the dollar depreciated to half its present value, that man would be able to pay his $2,000 mortgage with 2,000 fifty-cent dollars, but the insurance company when his policy becomes due could pay him off with
3,000	fifty-cent dollars. Will that help the farmers? I do not think so. He will find that the rule works both ways. In the subamendment there is a suggestion to go back to the time when the debts were incurred, to a period of inflation. Is it not strange that these debts were incurred during a period of inflation, and yet my friends in the corner ask for another period of inflation?
When are debts incurred? Certainly always during periods of inflation. If a man familiar with the economic history of the human race had twenty years ago been transported to the northern wilds and kept there in absolute ignorance of everything that has since happened in the world, and were brought back to-day and presented with a statement of the present debts of our people as compared with the debts we had twenty years ago, and were asked his explanation, his answer would be, "You must have gone through a period of inflation." It is always during periods of inflation that we get into debt. This is how

it works: money becomes cheap; every dollar is torn in two and each half is called a dollar. We are handling more counters. We think we are prosperous. Land values go up; every man tries to buy his neighbour out- goes into debt to do it. The price of stocks goes up-but not in real value, only in the number of counters. When stocks begin to go up everybody begins to speculate. We buy stocks in the morning at 50, and by night they have reached 60. Then we think we have made a profit of ten dollars. We feel rich and begin to live accordingly. Money is plentiful and easily borrowed; credit is easily obtained, and with that credit we buy more houses, more cars, finer furniture, finer clothes, consuming real wealth and giving worthless paper in exchange. That is the story of inflation. Inflate the currency again, and what will happen? There would be another boom in real estate, another boom in common stocks, another period of wild speculation, another period of living beyond our means. Then some fine morning we would wake up to find ourselves more hopelessly in debt than ever.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be the time to sell out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; everybody thinks he
will sell out just before the crash comes. The unfortunate fact is however that he does not do so. When one man sells another man usually buys. Somebody is always caught.
I think the most unjust and immoral suggestion that has been made in this house since I have been a member of it was made by the hon. member for Acadia when he suggested we should tax the savings of the people into circulation. These are his words:
If I were the minister of finance just for long enough to bring in the budget I would take the attitude that under present conditions we are justified in taxing those enormous savings into circulation.
I do not know what justification he can find for such a statement. We will suppose that two men working side by side receive their pay envelopes on Saturday night. One goes to town and spends his money, having a good time. The other takes a more serious view of life and says, "I will not spend all my money; I should like to save a little for my old age. I should like to educate my children when they grow up." He spends half his income and saves the other half. Surely he is entitled to his savings. If it is taken away from him, what happens? If we tax the savings of the people as suggested, we are taxing those men who make it possible for us to live in our houses. No man can build a house without

The Budget-Mr. Young
borrowing money, or at least using someone else's savings. A man either has to save his own money or use somebody else's if he intends to build. If that money is taxed and taken away from him, what will he do? He will have to live outside until he can build his own home. If you tax that money into circulation you say to the banks, "Give us the savings of the people." What will the people do? They will take their money out of the banks and put it into their stockings-the first national bank.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They might put it into government bonds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and encourage the government in its extravagance. How would you get that money into the hands of the unemployed? How are we to get it into the hands of those who cannot pay their debts? These are the questions with which we are faced. The people will say, "We cannot put our money into the banks, so we will put it into stocks."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or socks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stocks or socks, yes. If it is put into socks, it is hidden away and is of no use to anybody. If it is put into stocks-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would it be the socks the hon. member exhibited in the house last year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wishes to see those socks he may do so any time he likes. If he puts it into stocks he will be investing it in more plant and equipment to which my hon. friends in the comer object.
And now, for a moment, I should like to deal with the suggestion made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) to the effect that we might restore prosperity by artificially increasing the value of silver in its relation to gold. A few nights ago he made a very elaborate argument to prove that our trouble to-day is due to the fact that gold has become very dear. He said the fall in the price level had been the cause of all our trouble. As we measure everything by gold, a fall in price level means a rise in the price of gold. The minister says we can bring prosperity to China -w'hich uses silver as her standard-by doing the very thing with their standard that has been done with our standard, and has brought disaster upon us. He says we should artifically increase the price of silver in China. If an increase in the price of our standard has resulted in disaster in this country, would not an increase in the price of China's standard have the same effect in that country? He seems to labour under the impression that China buys
its imports with silver. China does not buy goods with silver; she buys silver with goods. China has no silver mines. She buys her silver from us, from Mexico, and other countries that produce it. If you artificially increase the price of silver you compel the Chinaman to give you more goods for the silver he wants. Can you restore prosperity to China in that way? I am afraid the Minister of Trade and Commerce was a little loose in his thinking on that occasion.
Coming now to the gold standard, are we or are we not on the gold standard? Some say we are not. We are not; and we are. In so far as redeeming our dollars in gold is concerned, we are not on the gold standard but in so far as measuring values is concerned, we are on the gold standard and we cannot get off it. Our values are still measured in gold, and when we divorced our dollar from gold, our dollar, still being measured in gold, dropped in value to eighty cents, the amount of gold it was worth. The law says so many grains of gold is a dollar, but the law does not say what that many grains of gold will buy, and when we said, "We won't give that many grains of gold in exchange for the dollar," then the business men of the world, and the public generally, the people said, "Well, we will give you for your dollars just exactly what it is worth in gold." I do not agree with the member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) when he says gold was chosen by Sir Robert Peel as the standard because it was pretty and could be cut up in pieces without hurting it. That was not the idea at all. Gold was chosen as the standard of value because in every country, in every age, and under all conditions, it was the one commodity that men were willing to take in exchange for whatever they had to sell. It did not matter what you wanted to sell, where you were, when or under what circumstances, you would always take gold for it. It did not matter what you were trying to buy, people would always be willing to accept payment in gold. The governments of the world in selecting gold as the standard of value simply said: "We recognize this condition which already prevails." That condition prevails, because, as my friends said, the metal has a certain quality in itself. It is imperishable; it is convenient to handle; it can be cut up without injury; it is attractive in ap-pearence.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the most useless metal mined.	.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Maybe, but the human race are willing to give work in exchange for it.
The Budget-Mr. Young

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You cannot make an axe out of it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say the human race are willing to take it in exchange for anything they have to sell, and it is the only thing they are willing to take in exchange. It is no concern of ours whether the metal is of any practical value or not, whether they want it to eat or to wear. The essential thing is that they are always willing to take it in exchange for what they have to sell. That is the reason why gold was chosen as a standard. It has an advantage too. Speaking broadly, the value of anything should be determined by the human labour required to produce it. It would be impossible to determine the value of one man's labour for a day against the value of every other man's labour for the same time, and it was necessary to find some commodity whose value was determined, as I said, speaking broadly, by the amount of labour required to produce it, and which varied in value very, very little. There is nothing produced in the world to-day that I know of the labour cost of whose production varies so little as that of gold. That is one of the great advantages of the gold standard. My friends object to it because it does not vary. They want a measure that does vary. But the mariner must always steer by a fixed star, not by a wandering comet. If we are going to determine the values of other things we must have something stable to measure them by. It would not do for us to measure to-day by a thirty-six inch yard stick and to-morrow by a thirty-eight inch yard stick. We want something that varies less than anything else
and gold is that thing. Those who would abolish the gold standard and put something else in its place must find some other commodity that has all the advantages of gold and that will not vary in labour cost any more than does gold.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are they doing in England just now?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I said, as a measure of value, England is not off the gold standard any more than we are. True, she is not redeeming her pound in gold, but gold is the measure of value to-day just the same as it was before, and that is the reason why the pound is down so low. Its value is being measured in gold and people will not give as much gold for it as formerly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is not the pound the measure of vailue. Not gold?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, gold is the real measure of value, and because the pound is not redeemable in gold it has lost its value.
Now, in regard to the proposal that we should nationalize our banks, again I say I cannot agree with the subamendment. What would you do if you nationalized the banks? You would have to set up some sort of body to control them. Who is going to control that body? Would you set that body up independent of everybody else, a self-perpetuating commission not answerable to anybody, and let that commission do as it liked with currency and credit? If not, then you will have to make them responsible to somebody. To whom will they be responsible ? To this house, to this parliament. And being responsible to parliament means being responsible to the government of the day. I ask my hon. friends in the corner if they would like to go into an election with all our 'banks under the control of my hon. friends opposite? Of recent days we have had some light cast on the inner workings of some of our government institutions. Don't you think there is too much political interference? Can you have such government control without political interference? If we made such a body responsible to the government, the government would be held responsible for their actions and they-the government-would have the right to control.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is my hon. friend trying to discredit the political party system?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I should like to quote a few words from John Stuart Mill's essay on Liberty in regard to this movement to put everything in the hands of government. He
says:
Every function superadded to those already exercised by the government causes its influence over hopes and fears to be more widely diifused, and converts, more and more, the active and ambitious part of the public into hangers-on of the government, or of some party which aims at becoming the government. If the roads, the railways, the banks, the insurance offices, the great joint-stock companies, the universities, and the public charities, were all of them branches of the government; if, in addition, the municipal corporations and local boards, with all that now devolves on them, became departments of the central administration; if the employees of all these different enterprises were appointed and paid by the government, and looked to the government for every rise in life; not all the freedom of the press and popular constitution of the legislature would make this or any other country free otherwise than in name. And the evil would be greater, the more efficiently and scientifically the administrative machinery was constructed-the more skilful the arrangements for obtaining the best qualified hands and heads with which to work it.

The Budget-Mr. Shaver
Further on he says:
If indeed all the high talent of the country could be drawn into the service of the government, a proposal tending to bring about that result might well inspire uneasiness. If every part of the business of society which required organized concert, or large and comprehensive views, were in the hands of the government, and if government offices were universally filled by the ablest men, all the enlarged culture and practised intelligence in the country, except the purely speculative, would be concentrated in a numerous bureaucracy, to whom alone the rest of the community would look for all things; the multitude for direction and dictation in all they had to do; the able and aspiring for personal advancement. To be admitted into the ranks-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has spoken forty minutes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will you iplease allow me to finish this sentence, Mir. Speaker?
To be admitted into the ranks of this bureaucracy, and when admitted, to rise therein, would be the sole objects of ambition. Under this regime, not only is the outside public ill-qualified, for want of practical experience, to criticize or cheek the mode of operation of the bureaucracy, but even if the accidents of despotic or the natural working of popular institutions occasionally raise to the summit a ruler or rulers of reforming inclinations, no reform can be effected which is contrary to the interest of the bureaucracy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire first of all to add my congratulations to those already extended by hon. members on both sides of the house to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the presentation of his first budget. The province from which he comes is comparatively small in area and perhaps small in population as compared with some of the other provinces of Canada, but it has given to the public life of this country many eminent statesmen, and I am quite sure that throughout Canada today there is no one who is regarded in higher esteem than the hon. gentleman who now holds the portfolio of finance, for which he is so eminently fitted by education, by training, by long political experience and, most of all, by great personal ability.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the long address delivered a few days ago by the hon. member for Shelbume-Yar-mouth (Mr. Ralston), the chief financial critic of the opposition. His remarks have been echoed and reechoed-sometimes the echoes were rather hollow-by hon. gentlemen apposite who followed. I noticed that his remarks were absolutely one-sided, and I was particularly interested in one observation he made, which appears on page 1421
of Hansard. Criticizing a speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), the hon. member stated that he had substituted information for argument. When I heard that remark I did not think it could be possible, and I verified it my consulting Hansard; I did not believe a man could be criticized for substituting information for argument. Information presented in logical order which is the method always followed by the Prime Minister, is the very best of arguments, and the speech of the Minister of Finance owned its strength to the fact that it was a presentation of that character. After looking through the long speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, which took nearly two and one-half hours to deliver, one must come to the conclusion that such criticism could not be applied to him, as his speech contained the maximum amount of argument built up on the minimum of information.
One of the criticisms levelled against the present government by many hon. gentlemen opposite who have taken part in this debate is the fact that Canada's foreign trade has declined since this government came into power. We all know that that is simply the result of world conditions, and that the foreign trade of every other country is also declining. I venture to say that if the comparisons were stated not in dollars but in tons, yards and cubic feet, in quantities rather than values, there would not be such a great discrepancy between the figures for 1931 and those for preceding years. The policy of the government now in power has placed the foreign trade of this country in a relatively better position when compared with other exporting and importing countries than it has been for many years past. In a period of depression-we can make a correct estimate of whether our foreign trade is advancing or receding only by comparing it with the trade of other nations. According to the statistics for 1930, the last year in which hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, our country was fifth among the importing countries of the world, and in sixth position when exports were considered. In 1931, under the protective policy of the present government, we had dropped to sixth place among the importing countries but had risen to fifth place among the exporting countries. In 1930 we occupied seventeenth position with regard to our favourable trade balance, the favourable relation of exports and imports, but in 1931 we have moved up to fourteenth position. There is absolutely nothing in the arguments advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite in an effort to discredit
The Budget-Mr. Shaver

the government because our foreign trade had declined.
Attempts have been made during the last and present sessions to belittle the work of the Prime Minister at the imperial conference. We were told by practically every hon. member opposite who spoke last session-some have referred to it during the present session -that the Prime Minister had made a great mistake when he proposed that Great Britain should adopt a protective tariff, that such an attitude would result in nothing but failure as far as the results of the economic conference were concerned. The major and minor prophets on the opposite side of the house said that Great Britain would never forsake her old policy of free trade. There now seems to be a pathetic look on the faces of some hon. gentlemen opposite-rather like the expression of a man who has been betrayed in the house of a friend-when they realize that the last country in the world to which they could look to carry on free trade, and from which they derived all the shibboleths they proclaimed so loudly during 'the election, has forsaken the policy she followed for so long and has become a protected country. I am reminded of the remark made on one occasion by the great Disraeli when he described a political opponent as a man who was distinguished among his colleagues because he possessed only one idea, and that idea was wrong. As far as economic ideas are concerned I am sure that many hon. gentlemen opposite possess only one, that of free trade, and it has been proven to be wrong by the greatest exemplar of free trade.
I regret the many attacks which have been made against the manufacturers of this country. It has seemed almost impossible for some hon. members to make a speech without making deprecatory remarks about our manufacturers. They have been referred to as the protected vested interests, as those receiving special benefits from the government, and so on; but coming from a constituency in which there are several large industries, knowing what has been done by industry generally and realizing that no other class deserves the thanks of the Canadian people to a greater extent than the manufacturers, I desire to protest against this attitude. During this period of depression through which we are passing no class has been readier to make sacrifices, and to take such steps as would enable men and women to earn a decent living, than has the manufacturer. I am not concerned so much with the manufacturers as I am with the four thousand men and women in my own county who are making a living

in industry and who are enabled to keep their families in comfort and send their children to school because they have had steady jobs since this government came into power. I know it is difficult to touch the hearts of some hon. gentlemen opposite by making an appeal on this basis. There may be hon. gentlemen who would prefer to buy agricultural implements manufactured in a country other than Canada, who would rather drive an American automobile than one made in Canada, who would prefer to use in their homes cotton goods made in the southern states or in Czechoslovakia rather than in the mills in my own county; who would prefer socks made in Japan to those made in Canada; and I know it is difficult to touch the hearts of such hon. members by making an appeal on behalf of the four thousand working men and women in my county. However, I do appeal to them at least to be reasonable and to give the manufacturers a fair show.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Resuming where I left off
when the house rose at six o'clock, I would refer for a few moments to the taxation proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance in the recent budget. Every hon. member, I presume, is interested in the reaction of his own constituents to these proposals; he is anxious to know whether they have received them with satisfaction or the contrary. The hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. McGillis), whose constituency is next to mine, and I have received several letters from those whom we represent, strongly approving of the taxation proposals contained in the budget. The Cornwall Freeholder of April 9 had a series of interviews with prominent business men in that town, about equally divided between the two political parties, and while there were some minor criticisms of a few secondary points in the budget, they agreed in the main entirely that these taxation proposals are fair and equitable and so adjusted as to fall on those best able to bear them. I will read one paragraph of an interview with one of the prominent business men of that town. He said:
We must appreciate the fact that the government must balance its budget, and that the money must come out of the public. I believe that the budget taxation is chiefly aimed to take the most revenue out of those best able to afford it.

The Budget-Mr. Shaver
That is a clear indication that the majority, at any rate, of the people in my constituency are thoroughly satisfied with the taxation proposed in the budget, particularly in this period of depression through which the country is passing.
Returning now to a consideration of the conditions of industry in Canada, a question which I touched upon briefly before six o'clock, I think that one indication of the progress of industry is supplied in the number of failures in industry in Canada, comparing 1930 with 1931. In 1930, the last year in which hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, there were 2,402 commercial failures in Canada, and in 1931 the number had decreased to 2,216. The Bureau of Statistics informs us that 141 new industries of outside origin have been established in Canada since September, 1930, without taking into account any of the additions made to industries already in existence. Everyone in this house knows the beneficial effect on the automobile industry. For several weeks, in fact extending over a period of two or three months, we frequently saw in the newspapers reports of American automobile firms, one after another establishing branch plants in Canada, many of which are now in operation. The hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. MacNicol), in the excellent address he delivered in this house the other evening, gave a very clearcut and comprehensive idea of the advantage which the changes made in the tariff by the present government have brought to the iron and steel industry. The hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards) similarly explained in full the beneficial effect of the present tariff on the knitted goods and woollen industry of this country. These are two phases of industry that have been actually benefited. But I would refer hon. gentlemen to an authority entirely outside Canada, an authority wholly unbiassed and one who has no political preferences so far as Canada is concerned. The following appeared in a despatch dated Washington, D.C., April 14, 1932, and published in the morning newspapers of that day:
Administration economic experts definitely attribute the expansion of American industrial branches in Canada to the influence of the Canadian tariff policy. The branch factory movement has been considerably retarded by the depression, except in the case of Canada, where it has been maintained primarily by the pressure of a definite tariff policy.
That is the opinion of Dr. F. B. Feiker, of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Relations of the United States.
I would refer more especially to conditions obtaining in my own county. Last year, in a
speech I made in this house, I told of the benefits derived by the industries of Cornwall, and those outside the town, from the tariff policy of the present government. I am very glad to ibe able to tell the house that that improvement in industry has been maintained during the past year. I have here part of a report of the president of the board of trade which was printed in the Cornwall Freeholder of February 6, 1932, dealing with industrial conditions in the town' in the year 1931. This is a very clear and comprehensive report under the heading, "Some improvement in conditions here during past year". I will read one paragraph dealing with industry:
I now pass to statistical information concerning the industrial phases of our town and the surrounding district. The collective figures for fourteen of our industries are as follows: number of men employed. 3,353; amount of wages and salaries, $3,036,591.58; value of finished products, $12,264,377.48. This is a very slight decrease from last year and it is due to the fact that I am able to report for fourteen industries only, whereas last year, figures for seventeen industries were given. In has been impossible for us to get the figures of the remaining three industries, and should we have had them, there is no doubt that there would have been a slight increase over last year.
I am sure that in this period of world depression, when the president of a board of trade of any town is able to report a slight improvement in industry in 1931, it is a matter .that must be gratifying to the Canadian people and especially to those of us on this side of the house. I mentioned last year that one of the largest industries in my county, Court-auld'fe Limited, rayon manufacturers, were constructing an addition to their plant, costing 82,000,000, and giving employment to 300 men during the winter of 1931. That addition to their plant has now been in operation for several months, and whereas when this government came into power 1,000 persons were on its payroll, there are now 1,400, working full time.
The hon. member for Toronto Northwest mentioned the beneficial effect which one successful industry had on others throughout the country, supplying that particular industry with the various chemicals and raw materials it used. As an indication of that truth, this industry to which I refer used last year over three-quarters of a million dollars' worth of Canadian materials including wood pulp from such widely separated parts of the country as Temiskaming, Ontario, and Campbellton, New Brunswick; coal from Nova Scotia; chemicals from Sulphide, Ontario, from Windsor and Montreal, and various other materials from other points.
The Budget-Mr. Shaver

Let me mention the fine paper industry, represented by two mills in the county of Stormont. By the abolition of tariff item 1060, in the short session of 1930, those industries were greatly helped and encouraged. They received many orders from Canadian magazine publishers, who had formed}' received under the terms of that item a rebate of eighty per cent of the duty on paper purchased in the United States. The concerns in question received a good deal of additional business that way. Further, in consequence of the tariff changes made at the last regular session, many American magazine publishers were forced to come into Canada and publish here. That has also brought a good deal of additional business to these mills. In addition to that, stimulation of business in other industries has been occasioned by the tariff policy of the present government, and that has meant a good deal of business for the fine paper industry.
With reference to cotton textiles, which are represented by three mills in my county, it is a fact well known to anyone who has looked into the matter, that since the war there has been a world-wide overproduction of cotton textiles. That is true of nearly every country in the world that manufactures textiles of this kind, except Canada. To show clearly that there has been no overproduction in this country, I would point out that in 1930 the production of the Canadian cotton mills was, in money, $58,587,366; but we imported in the year ended March 31, 1931, $22,634,074 worth of cotton textiles. This proves that there has been no overproduction in Canada; on the contrary, there is great room for expansion in that industry. Let me show how this industry was gradually languishing under the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. In 1929 the production of the cotton mills of Canada amounted to $90,079,956, and, as I said before, it dropped in 1930 to $58,587,366. There was a corresponding reduction in capital investment, number of employees and salaries and wages paid. I have not been able to obtain complete figures for 1931, so that I cannot give a comparison showing the result of the policy of the present government on that industry as a whole in Canada, but I am able to give a comparison as regards the mills in my constituency, and they show a very clear and definite improvement. This table shows the production of manufactured cotton in mills in my county in 1930, the last year hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and that in 1931:
Year	Production

That shows an increase of 556,137 pounds or 8i per cent, so that it is apparent the industry has been materially benefited.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite have compared prices; they have told us that prices on manufactured products have not declined to the same extent as those of the products of the farm. That is very true. It is something that always happens when there is a decline in prices, and that everyone deplores; but at the same time the reduction in the price of manufactured products has been much greater than hon. gentlemen have stated in the figures they have given to the house. In a short speech which I delivered a few weeks ago, I pointed out the reduction in price on various items as given to me by one of the leading merchants in my county, a gentleman who has been in business for a long time, who keeps accurate records and who is able to give a clear and correct computation of the reduction in prices. His figures show that in the last two years there have been the following reductions:
Commodity	Reduction in price
Dry goods	 22 to 25 per cent
Boots and shoes	 18 to 20 per cent
I notice the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) said that there had been a decline in price of 4.6 per cent on boots and shoes, and his figures were confirmed by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott). If they had visited some manufacturers or wholesale merchants or had bought a pair of shoes of the kind they were accustomed to buy two years ago, I am sure they would have found the reduction was much more than that. A gentleman who has a very wide connection with the furniture trade told me that furniture had decreased in price at least 25 per cent.
I wish also to place on Hansard a comparison compiled from figures on sales slips in the country store in which I am a partner. I am comparing prices in January, 1930, on goods on an actual sales slip of that date with prices on the same goods in January, 1932. I have several sales slips, but I have time to place only one on Hansard. I select this one because it consists entirely of manufactured goods, as follows: two pairs of rubbers, one suit underwear, five yards of ticking, pair of overalls, two pairs of woollen socks. The prices are as follows:
Date	Price

January, 1932	 8 10
That shows a reduction of 26.36 per cent, proving conclusively there has been a great reduction in prices of manufactured goods.

I noticed during the course of this debate, although perhaps not to the same extent as a year ago, some hon. gentlemen opposite are still holding post mortems on their defeat in 1930; they are still blaming New Zealand butter for that wonderful landslide which took place in July, 1930. They have only themselves to blame, they had placed themselves in a position where there wras no possibility of escape. For four years prior to the last general election they were telling the people from the public platform, in the press and on the floor of parliament that large quantities of New Zealand butter coming into Canada were not detrimental, but in a sense beneficial to our dairy farmer. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) has been using that argument during the present session. The Canadian farmer, who in their opinion apparently did not know his own business we'll enough to control his production, had to be warned away from getting on the foreign market, protected from doing so, by the method of allowing butter from countries which could produce it more cheaply to come into Canada at a low rate of duty or under no duty at all. My hon. friends opposite used that argument until a few weeks of the election; then they brought down the Dunning budget and reversed everything they had said1 during the previous four years. They placed a duty on butter and gave notice of the abrogation of the agreement with New Zealand.
At that time I was making a personal canvass of the electorate in my constituency. I had been at this work for a couple of weeks, and the morning after the Dunning budget came down I noticed a different attitude amongst the farmers. They were convinced already-no argument on my part was needed -that the government which those of them who were Liberals were following, was entirely wrong, because they had admitted this by their

Hon. gentlemen opposite have told us about the low price of farm products and have endeavoured to lay the blame for that on the government of today. In my constituency I never told anyone that the Canadian price would be raised if world prices declined, but I said to the farmers that they were going to have fair and equal competition in their own markets; they were to have a chance to supply the people of Canada with butter made in this country. That was the argument I used.
The low price of farm products is common throughout the whole world, but I think I can prove conclusively the action which the present government has taken has been of great assistance in maintaining prices of farm products at a higher level than would have been the case had hon. gentlemen opposite remained in power. There is no question that their policy of admitting farm products of different kinds at very low rates of duty had the effect of keeping down the price at different periods of the year when there would be a chance from various causes for prices to rise; there was always this influence of a large quantity of foreign commodities coming on the market. I have under my hand a comparison of price reductions in Canada and in the United States, and I think it is a fair one. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on the fact that his budget speech was on such a high plane and couched in cultured and dignified language befitting the occasion, that occasion being the presentation to the shareholders of Canada of their annual statement of accounts.
Of primary importance in the budget is the increase in the income tax. I wish to congratulate the minister on his income tax proposals, not simply because he has increased the tax, nor because I like to see an increase in the taxes of someone else beside myself, but because I believe that when we must have additional revenue the income tax is the very surest way of securing it; it is also the fairest tax because it is based purely on the principle of ability to pay.
Perhaps I may be permitted to put on record a few figures to show that the income tax is capable of being used still further as a revenue producer. I will give first the figures of the income tax for 1921, when the present government went out of office, about the end of the war period; the reductions made in income tax in the last regime, and the new income tax, which is still considerably lower than the tax as it was in 1921. The figures that I shall quote are for a married person without children :
Income	Tax 1921	Tax 1930	New tax	$ 10.000	$ 619 50	$ 232 00	$ 354	9020.000	2.089 50	1,232 00	1.730	4030.000	4.084 50	2,880 00	3.918	60100,000	32.749 50	19,064 00	25.248	30200,000	97,849 50	51,496 00	67,859	4041761-1341	
I think, Mr. Speaker, these figures will show that the income tax is capable of being used still further, provided that additional revenue is required another year.
I wish again to express my appreciation of the fact that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to postpone for another year the imposition of the increased duties on implement repairs, and I hope by the time another year has come round he will see fit to cancel them altogether. In this section of the house, where hon. members are so very much concerned with the matter of implement repairs, we appreciate the minister's action very much indeed. This budget stands in a -class by itself, and enjoys the unique distinction of containing no increases in the tariff, and only one decrease. The reasons are of course fairly obvious. I presume on account of the approaching Imperial economic conference -the government is postponing alterations until that time. For that reason we appreciate all the more the fact that the minister has made -this one exception by postponing the imposition of the duty on implement -repairs.
There is just one other feature to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister, namely the method of application of the so-called excise tax. This is increased from one to three per cent, and as it applies only to imports it really -constitutes an increase in the tariff. My understanding of an excise tax is that it should apply equally on home products and imported goods. In this case the minister is sim-ply following the example set by the Minister of Finance for the year 1926, the late Hon. Mr. Robb, who, I think for the first -time, made the excise tax on motor cars applicable only to imported cars, amounting to an increase in protection.
I think I may safely state that so far as we can now see the outstanding event in the year will be the Imperial economic conference. People in all parts of the British empire are looking forward with hope and confidence to the conference, and I trust the Canadian government will not disappoint the people of Canada or of other parts of the empire by failing to do its share to measure up to expectations. Any disappointment or failure of the conference to measure up to the hopes of the people will indeed be serious. Disappointment would mean reaction, and would have an adverse psychological effect on business. I suggest that the government be prepared-probably they are; but there is no harm in suggesting that they go to the conference prepared to make some substantial
The Budget-Mr. Campbell

reductions in duties on British imports. It seems to me that unless they are ready to do that so far as we are concerned the conference will come to an end. If we expect to secure preferred treatment in the British market for our wheat, butter, cattle, lumber, copper or the many other products of Canada, we must be prepared to meet them in a spirit of fair play and make substantial reductions in the tariff on certain classes of British goods.
When we survey the schedules we cannot help thinking that textiles will be one of the commodities British people will be expecting to ship to Canada. The textile industry is being more carefully nurtured and better protected than any other industry in Canada. Some lines in connection with the textile industry are not indigenous to this country, and we should be prepared to make some concession to British interests in that regard.
I should like to say a word or two concerning the St. Lawrence deep waterway. From one end of Canada to the other there is considerable discussion as to whether or not this project is feasible, but I believe the consensus of opinion throughout Canada is that it is a practicable proposition. From the standpoint of both transportation and power it seems to me that the completion of that project would be a good thing for Canada. At the present time materials and labour are cheaper than they have been for a quarter of a century, and this is an opportune time to go ahead with and complete the work. Cheap material and cheap labour would be available, with resulting lower overhead and lower costs of power and transportation for all time to come. Already part of the scheme has been completed. We have the great Welland canal, the construction of which cost about S125.000,-000, and the Beauhamois canal, now almost completed, at a cost of about $20,000,000, ownership of which has been vested in the federal government. In any arrangement made with the .United States, Canada would be entitled to a cash credit for her interest in parts already completed, and that is something we may well take into consideration. I do not listen to many of the extravagant predictions concerning reduced rates on our grain and other commodities, put forward by those favouring the project. Undoubtedly many unwarranted and extravagant statements are being made in that connection, but I feel quite sure that from the standpoint of transportation the completion of the project is fully justified.
Then we must consider the development of power. Cheap power is the basis of industry.

The more cheap power we can put on the market in Canada the more likely we are to bring industries from other lands. I do not believe I am overstating the facts when I say that to-day Canada has more potential water power than all the rest of the world put together. It seems to me that by a proper development of that power, seeing to it that the overhead in the development is not too great, we can lay a foundation for the greatest industries Canada and the world has ever seen. I may be looking ahead some distance, but I am convinced that Canada has greater opportunities in that respect than any other country in the world. The distribution of money, the employment of labour necessary in the construction of a work of this kind, would be a stimulus to industry and have beneficial effects all round. In addition undoubtely the government would be saved the expenditure of millions of dollars in unemployment relief. Practically the only market we have to look forward to for our wheat is Great Britain, but I still believe the United States is the logical market for many of the products of our farms, our forests and our mines, and it is a market of which I hope we shall ultimately secure a fair share. The completion of arrangements for the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway should be a powerful factor in creating more harmonious relations between Canada and the United States-relations which would, I trust, ultimately result in trade arrangements to the mutual benefit of both countries.
May I draw attention more particularly to the Liberal amendment. It simply asks for a reduction of tariff, I presume back to the position where it stood when the Liberals -left office in 1930. Quite obviously this is not sufficient to cope with the present depression. The moving of such a meek and anaemic amendment was not a fitting end to the very able presentation of the case for his party made by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). In looking over this amendment in the face of the very serious problems confronting us to-day, I would say it is utterly unworthy of the great traditions of the Liberal party.
On the other hand, the subamendment goes to the very root of present day conditions. Of first consideration in dealing with the depression is the condition of agriculture. In this connection I should like to place upon Hansard some figures from the Economic Annalist, a publication issued by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir):

It will also be noted that the index figure for farm field products to-day is just about twenty-five per cent of what it was in 1920. This was about the time when, I believe, the great bulk of the- debts of our western farmers, were incurred, so it can easily be seen what a desperate position our farmers are in to-day with respect to those debts.
