I draw attention to the fact that while these retail prices dropped only about fifteen per cent from 1926 to February of this year, field products dropped fifty-seven per cent. This will show one of the reasons why agriculture is adversely affected to a much greater extent than other industries.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in the very able and very excellent speech he gave us a few nights ago dealt with the money question. I wish to congratulate him on the study he has made of this question, and for the moral courage he had to express the opinions he did from the government benches. I -would say that he is the first federal cabinet minister who has ever attacked the money problem from that angle. He stated that there were four factors in the present depression-price levels, debt, interest and trade. In dealing with the fluctuating value of money and showing its effects on liabilities and debts, he asked the pertinent question as to what would happen if the system of weights and measures fluctuated as have commodity values during the last few years. He told us that what we needed today more than anything else was stability of prices. I may say that the minister's speech was almost a complete endorsation of the subamendment, because that is exactly what is aimed at. The minister did imply -that it would be necessary to have an international agreement to bring about any stabilization of commodity prices and to correct the evils in
the money system. I quite agree with him that we cannot deal with this question fully outside of an international agreement, but I do contend that if we sit here and wait until there is an international agreement arrived at nothing will ever be done. We in Canada can correct the position to a very large extent even without assistance from the outside world at all. Let us take the position of France in the depression of 1920-21. I do not think it will be contradicted by anyone that the international bankers' association agreed on a general deflation in 1920 ini order to bring the various countries back to the gold basis. Arrangements were made to have this brought about concurrently throughout the great countries of the world. The United States bankers deflated and they put six million men out of work, involving great misery, suffering and hardship. The English bankers deflated, two million men were put out of work, and they have been unemployed ever since. We know what happened in Canada. We had a period of very great distress, not so serious as the depression we are going through now, but very serious indeed. But the action of the French government is worthy of our attention. The government of France forbade their bankers to deflate as the bankers did in the other great countries, and while in- other countries prices were tumbling and men were thrown out of work with all the consequent hardship, misery and suffering, commodity prices remained fairly stable in France throughout that period, and every single man was working. As a matter of fact, while two million men were out of work in England, and six million were unemployed in the United States, France was bringing in workmen from Poland and the other eastern countries of Europe to keep her industries running.
An horn. MEMBER:	They are not doing
it now.

speechtext:
I quite understand that, but France did pull through that period much better than any other country in the world, largely because she refused to follow the
The Budget-Mr. Campbell

general deflation policy of the international bankers and maintained the level of prices. It was not until 1927 that France went back on the gold basis, and she did it then by establishing her currency at 25 per cent of its normal value. That meant writing off about 75 per cent of her national debt, but she did not strangle her industries; she kept her people working. That action of the French government should be an object lesson to Canada and to all other countries in the world. It seems to me that the preferred position in which France finds herself to-day is due to the action taken at that time by the government. After reducing her debts, after refusing to deflate and to go back to the gold basis, France to-day is the second largest holder of gold and she is almost supreme in dictating the financial policies of the rest of the world. If that means anything, it means that in Canada we can do the same thing regardless of whether or not there is an international agreement.
I do not need to take up the time of the house in discussing the relationship of the amount of money in circulation to commodity price levels. I think it is generally recognized to-day that the commodity price level is determined by the amount of money in circulation. This afternoon the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) criticized severely the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) in connection with his subamendment. The hon. member stated that it is absolutely necessary to have gold in order to maintain stability of prices, but I would say to him that the value of gold is fluctuating from day to day. This is a recognized fact among world economists. A short time ago thirty-eight cents in gold was all that was necessary to maintain the United States on a gold basis; to-day it takes about eighty cents. The standard of measurement has simply been lengthened. Gold to-day is one of the most useless metals; gold hidden away and sealed in the vaults in New York is performing no useful function. We have got into the habit of worshipping gold, and until we get away from that habit and get on to a sounder basis, we cannot expect to have prosperity in Canada.
The hon. member for Weyburn overlooked another factor with which this subamendment proposes to deal, and that is the relationship between commodities and debts. Debts were contracted when money was at a low valuation and now that we have almost quadrupled the value of money we have to pay three or four times the amount borrowed. This applies equally to public and private debts. One

object of the subamendment is to bring about the return of a proper relationship between commodity values and debts, to bring about the relationship which existed at the time the debts were created. As a matter of fact, there is no other way of paying these debts; going on as we are going on to-day simply means cancellation. My hon. friend probably would throw up his hands in horror at the suggestion of a general cancellation of debts, but we are on the horns of a dilemma-we must either inflate and get back to higher commodity levels in order to pay our debts, or we must cancel many of our debts. There is no middle course; we must choose either the one or the other. May I be permitted to quote a recognized authority in these matters, the Royal Bank of Canada, one of the largest banks in Canada. Dealing with the depression, their monthly letter said:
The present depression is usually explained in terms of extravagance, overproduction, excessive tariff barriers, etc., but, speaking generally the controlling influence has been the mismanagement of money and credit.
Could anything be more striking, coming as it does from one of the largest banks in Canada?
I direct the attention of the house to the fact that we have in Canada to-day the largest amount of bank deposits we have ever had in the history of the country. The latest figures for February show that these deposits amount to SI,390,000,000, and the increase from January to February amounted to S22,000,000. In some quarters this fact is considered as evidence of stability and prosperity; as a matter of fact it means the very opposite, it is an indication of business stagnation. If there were good investments available in business, this money would soon find its way into those channels. The hon. member for Acadia dealt with this particular question, and it is one of the points upon which he was severely criticized by the hon. member for Weyburn. The hon. member for Acadia suggested that these deposits be taxed into circulation, but I think the hon. member for Weyburn had an entirely wrong impression of what was being aimed at. The hon. member for Acadia was suggesting that something must be done to get this money into circulation, to get it working. For instance, only a short time ago the province of Alberta had to pay nearly 7 per cent on a loan issue. Just imagine-a provincial government having to pay nearly 7 per cent interest; and I understand there were additional inducements in the way of tax exemptions and other guarantees of that kind. Ontario, the wealthiest province in Canada, had to pay 6)

The Budget-Mr. McDade
per cent interest on a loan recently floated. All this at a time when there is more money in the savings banks of Canada than ever before! Is it not reasonable to suggest that some governmental action should be taken, not to turn this money into speculative channels, as suggested by the hon. member for Weybum, but into investment channels in municipal and government bonds?
I have another suggestion to make. Supposing the government were to set a maximum interest rate to be charged by the banks? If that rate was a reasonably low one, the banks in turn would be forced to reimburse themselves by reducing the rate of interest paid on deposits. When the depositor found his interest rate cut down to li or 2 per cent, he would probably buy some good Ontario, Alberta or Saskatchewan bonds, or perhaps the federal government bonds. That is one of the important things which we have to face to-day; we need a lower rate of interest on government loans. However, the main object of the subamendment was to increase the money in circulation and thus stimulate business and cause the rise of the commodity price level. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out, a rise in prices means a corresponding decrease in debts, both public and private.
A short time ago the members of this house were treated to a very excellent address by a distinguished gentleman from the old country, Sir Josiah Stamp. Sir Josiah Stamp is not a mere theorist or student, he is one of the biggest business men in England, being a director of the Bank of England and of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway. Perhaps I could not pay him a higher tribute than to quote the words used by the Prime Minister in introducing Sir Josiah. The Prime Minister referred to him as the greatest and soundest mind dealing with world affairs ever known.

I shall come to that in a moment. He predicted that England would not return to the gold standard; as a matter of fact, he suggested that England should reduce still further the value of her money. He said there would be no prosperity in England until they got back to the 1929 price level, and in order to get back to the 1929 price level there would have to be further inflation and a further reduction in the value of the pound. Sir Josdah did not attempt to tell us how to run our business in Canada, but his inference was strong. He said something to which this house and the people of Canada might well pay attention; the words of a gentleman who merits the praise applied to him by the Prime Minister should be taken seriously.
In conclusion, I should like to quote another authority, the monthly review issued by the Midland Bank of London, England. This is the most powerful bank in the world, and, dealing with the depression, this is what it says, in part:
Humanity is notoriously slow to learn by its own mistakes and inefficiency. It is easy to cry to heaven and denounce the slump as an act of God. But the old proverb still holds good, that heaven helps those who help themselves. A first task in self help is to devise a sure means of regulating the commodity price level and thus to avoid the repetition of a large part of the troubles we have brought upon ourselves.

speechtext:
May I join heartily in the congratulations extended to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), on his elevation to this most important portfolio. The hon. gentleman has had a long and distinguished career in the public life of Canada. For a time he held the high position of Speaker of this assembly, and afterwards was Prime Minister of his native province of Nova Scotia, both of which offices he occupied in an eminently satisfactory manner.
The matter of paramount importance before this house for some time seems to have been the unemployment situation. May I be permitted to dwell briefly on some phases of the subject, particularly as it affects the province of New Brunswick and the county of Northumberland, the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house. We all appreciate the fact that the present depression is world-wide. Some of my good friends opposite, in the course of a discussion that took up about three weeks, seemed to lose sight of the fact that conditions in Canada are no exception to those that obtain in many other countries to-day. As a matter of fact, conditions are better in Canada than in other countries, due reasonably to the sound policies of this administration. I submit, therefore, that it is unfair and illogical to attach any blame to the present government for the existing depression and distress which we find generally in this country. It is, I repeat, a worldwide condition.
Coming particularly to the province of New Brunswick, I may say that there was expended under the 1931 regulations on a contributory basis, on unemployment relief works, the sum of $2,165,020. This, I submit, is a record of which we may be proud. We could not have
The Budget-Mr. McDade

So far as federal expenditures under the unemployment relief fund in the county of Northumberland are iconcemed, no politics whatever was practised by the hon. member who happens to occupy that seat at the present time. As a matter of fact some of my good friends, particularly on the north side of the Miramichi river, saw fit to call a meeting and pass a vote of censure upon the member because he did not see fit to interfere in the handling of unemployment expenditures.

May I foe permitted to say a word respecting the Canadian National Railways? I wish to congratulate the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) upon the very substantial reduction that has already 'been effected in operating costs. I am sorry that I am not in agreement with the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) in his statement that the Canadian National railway system should be sold to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. We from the province of New Brunswick would be opposed to such a proposal unless and until we receive the report of the Duff commission, which has made a careful investigation into the various ramifications of the railway situation and which will be qualified to submit a fair and impartial report. At the same time I wish to say a word for the Canadian National Steamships. I have it on reasonably high authority that next year there will be a sufficient operating profit to discharge not only the operating expenses, but also the interest on the debt incurred. While I am on the subject, I should like to urge upon the Minister of Railways the desirability of including in the small special committee-the executive committee of management-one of the directors from the maritime provinces. We in the maritimes are great admirers of the Minister of Railways, and we feel that as the Intercolonial was the pioneer part of the Canadian National railway system, and particularly as we have such important questions affecting the great ports of St. John and Halifax, the minister and the management might reasonably include in this subcommittee a representative from the maritime provinces.
A matter of outstanding moment to-day in world politics, particularly in empire politics, is the approaching economic conference. I wish to congratulate the distinguished Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) and his colleagues on bringing this important economic conference to the capital city. May I humbly suggest that we approach the conference in a quid pro quo attitude; that we be prepared to give reasonable concessions in exchange for preferences in the mother country. Of especial interest to us on the north shore of New Brunswick is the policy of the administration to endeavour to secure preference for Canadian lumber. Lumber on the north shore of our province is our basic industry. It is indeed regrettable that private enterprise on the Miramichi is not doing more. The once great activity of lumbering operations which characterized this river some twelve or fifteen years ago is now practically negligible. Last year only 23,000,000 feet were cut, including a large number of ties by the Canadian National, large quantities of lumber supplied

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
to the St. John, harbour reconstruction, and valuable orders from the Canadian National Railways. This shows that private enterprise is not acting reasonably in the present economic crisis. Canada's timber supply is estimated to be 424,637,000,000 feet board measure of raw material and 1,121,933,000 cords of small material such as pulpwood, fuel wood, posts and so forth. Fifty-five species of wood occur; 32 hardwoods and 23 softwoods. Forest wealth, including accessible raw materials, and pulpwood and capital invested in forestry operations, is estimated to be $1,866,000,000. Annual production from the forests is valued at $500,000,000. Exports of wood, wood products and paper in 1930-31 amounted to $230,514,474.
I quote those figures, Mr. Speaker, to afford some indication of what a preference for Canadian lumber in the great market of the mother country would mean to this industry. In discussing this matter may I be permitted to observe that crown land timber leases in the province of New Brunswick will expire as of August 31, 1933. This is a very important phase of the question and it is to be hoped that the government of New Brunswick will give fearless, honest and intelligent attention to the renewal of those licences. Our democracy is such that if the American company now holding practically a monopoly of the leases does not see fit to operate the crown lands, those lands should be taken away from them and given to bona fide operators who will go ahead and1 operate.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that thoughtful and intelligent people are prepared to support this administration upon its achievements. Great problems have been attacked. A favourable trade balance has been established. New trade treaties have been negotiated, vigorous action has been taken to stimulate agriculture. The railway problem is being investigated by a board of experts. Unemployment has been grappled with and to a great extent eliminated. Tariff changes have already brought into this country many new industries. A report on the great harbours and seaports of Canada has been submitted by an eminent British authority. Another eminent authority has reported relative to trading in grain futures. The port facilities of St. John, which were destroyed by fire, have been rebuilt and are now bigger and better than ever. Civil service problems and radio are receiving careful study. Public men charged with irregularities have been forced to face investigation. Without impairing the efficiency of the service, the most drastic economy has been put into practice, and above all, the budget has been balanced for the ensuing year.
In spite of all this there is considerable misery and suffering in the country. These are dark days for Canada and the world, but all is not lost; we still have God. When those sacred and fundamental principles of Christianity have been attacked it is well that we should accept the challenge and effectively combat it. We have in the distinguished and illustrious Prime Minister of this country a man standing firmly by those Christian principles. Can there be any doubt, Mir. Speaker, of our ultimate success and triumph? The times always produce the man, and my native province of New Brunswick has had the honour of giving to Canada, to the empire and to the world a noble character, a brilliant leader and a self-renunciating statesman whose policies and whose principles will 'bring Canada to immeasurable prosperity and restore happiness to our great Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I wish, at the outset, to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), on his clear and methodical statement on the budget. However, owing to the necessarily incomplete nature of his statement, it is true to say that the discussion of it is difficult. Not having noted any tariff changes and being aware that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is convinced that Providence alone can solve our problems, and that he reposes no faith in the parliament of Canada to assist him-basing such a statement on the Act, No. 58, by which he assumes all executive and legislative powers, I therefore contend that this budget is certainly incomplete and brought down simply to follow the sessional custom.
Although deprived of our prerogatives, as long as the representatives of the people are allowed to meet in this chamber, under your presidency, sir, we shall continue to fulfil our duty, at least by making suggestions which we deem in the people's interests, since our cooperation is no more needed; and that is the course I intend to follow.
It is true that our financial position is seriously affected, but nevertheless, I do not think that our condition is so desperate as to prompt the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) to suggest to the Prime Minister to seize the savings of the people, savings which were accumulated, thanks to their thrift and sacrifices. The government can gradually bring about great reforms in the administration which will surely foster an appreciable degree of prosperity.
The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The
Treaty of Versailles has not succeeded in establishing peace among nations. President Wilson who first conceived the idea of founding a league of nations could not even get the United States to join. Ever since the outset of this institution the United States always opposed its proposals and never will they consent to pledge their responsibilty.
In 1923, when the project of mutual assurance came up, so as to give the necessary assistance to a nation attacked, a number of the great powers refused to endorse it. In 1925, a new attempt was made with the protocol of nations. This again was a failure. In 1925-26, the Locarno treaty was signed, the work of Mr. Briand, by which all nations were to pledge themselves to form a "bloc" against countries declaring war. Again this was a failure. Then follows the establishment of a tribunal at The Hague, to arbitrate disputes between nations. Again this was useless and always for the same reason because this tribunal had no power to enforce its decisions. The treaty of Versailles was amended, the Dawes' plan is adopted, then comes Young's plan; delays are granted for the payments of war reparations. A short while ago, Germany declared that she was unable to meet her payments; to-morrow she will clearly refuse to do so. We will then witness a number of nations anxious to have their loans repaid previous to war reparations, side with her. This is, in a nutshell to what the League of Nations amounts.
Can one possibly believe that "France has no cause to be fully armed and maintain friendly relations with the small European nations which she has freed from the German, Austrian or Hungarian yoke, and was also instrumental in having restored to them their territories, so unjustly cut up and tyrannically exploited. After The Hague tribunal, we have had the Briand-Kellogg pact signed by fifty-two nations and which can have no practical result when a well armed country goes to war. The fact is that a number of first class powers have not yet signed this treaty. All these institutions had a very laudable and friendly object in view. Their intentions were the very best. Nevertheless, they failed. To reach the aim which the League had in view, all nations should have joined it and it should have been entrusted with the power to carry out its decrees and, moreover, all nations forming part of the league have given evidence of their good faith. That is Mr. Tardieu's contentions.
After the failures which I have just enumerated, and without the conditions that I mentioned above, we are led to believe that all plans of disarmament so as to promote peace among nations, are purely utopian.
If the procedure of the League of Nations is closely studied, one easily discovers the lack of sincerity and good faith shown by some of its members. The United States in-
The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers

vented this sovereign remedy and, for twelve years, have fought shy of it. Are they sincere?
It is well known that Great Britain carries on trade with Russia, thus encouraging forced labour to compete with free labour and this during a crisis. It thus fosters a system of revolutionary government that all civilized nations condemn, precisely when this system has most need of this help to succeed. Did not the League of Nations itself approve of loans to this same Soviet republic? Yet, does not article 23 of the League of Nations oblige all those who signed the pact to endeavour to obtain satisfactory and human conditions of labour for men, women and children in all countries, and to resist forced labour? Is their attitude rational? Would not its duty be to leave to this dangerous power all its over production in order that its own citizens should fully benefit of this abundance?
To-day when conferences on disarmament are held, arms and machinery to manufacture them are being sold to Russia.
Faced with this series of uninterrupted failures of the League of Nations, including the Manchuria fiasco; bearing in mind the inconsistency of its members who pledge themselves [DOT] one day to follow a very determined line of action, and who, the very next day, do the contrary, are we not allowed to share the views of Mr. Eric Loow-a minister in the South African Union government -which were transmitted by the correspondent of the Canadian Press, in New York, in June, 1931. Mr. Loow stated that he was of the opinion that his country should resign from the League of Nations, adding that the latter had sadly failed in its negotiations regarding the conflict in Manchuria, in 19311932, as it would similarly fail in the future to settle any conflict in which the interests of a powerful nation were at stake; that the clear political tendencies of certain recent decisions of the international court had shocked and disgusted the most enthusiastic partisans of the league; that his observations, as head of the South African delegation to the meeting of the league in 1929, had convinced him that the league served as a lobby for intrigues, where most of the important questions are settled behind the scene, by way of underhand dealing, among the various great powers.
It is a known fact, in well informed circles, chat England wishes to do away with land armies, submarines and air forces, but that she will never consent to abandon her cruisers; that Italy intends to keep her land armies and the necessary navy to rule the 
Mediterranean sea. Germany claims equality of armament and has arranged to have her war material manufactured secretly in Holland, Scandinavia and Switzerland; Japan agrees with any peaceful movement, providing she is allowed to put the Chinese lords where they belong, through the mouth-piece of her guns; and the United States are bent on the disarmament of other nations. So that we are faced with nations more or less sincere, most of whom through interest, envy or simply stupidity seek to disarm France.
While Germany was taking part in the deliberations at Geneva-in the interest of world peace-on the anniversary of the Versailles treaty, June 28, 1931, the Reischwehr unveiled on the manoeuvring fields of Dobaritz, near Berlin, an enormous map of the world made of stone, over which the German Eagle soared, and bearing the following inscription: "German soil in the hands of foreigners: Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Pass, Upper-Silesia, Schleswig-Holstein, the Camer-ouns, the Togo, German South East and South West Africa." One need not be a prophet to foresee, through the numerous conferences on disarmament, that many a bloody battle will be fought before Germany reconquers all these territories. Going back a few years, we find Italy refusing the intervention of the League of Nations, at Corfu; then come the republics of South America settling their difficulties by the intermediary of the United States after having bluntly refused the good office of the League of Nations; it was powerless to prevent war between Russia and Poland; its influence was nil in the conflict between Italy and Jugo-Slavia; d'Annunzio laughed at it. Its intervention was limited to humbly requesting parties concerned to desist, it might just as well have requested lions to trim their claws, because, without the power to impose its will, it felt powerless.
Ambition, interest, hatred and vengeance are sentiments which are intimately linked with mankind and will survive, as long as nations exist; conferences, congresses, tribunals will always meet on their path these indestructible obstacles which render world peace impossible.
When we have witnessed while war was raging, Thyrsen, the Rothchilds, the Krupps at work, all moved by the same sordid feelings when their brothers were dying by the millions; it is but right to point out these despicable individuals concocting their diplomatic intrigues in lobbies, hidden in large hotels, and spoiling the plans devised for the welfare of those concerned. I was most amazed in reading in the Senate Hansard of March 10, 1932, a statement of a former dele-

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
gate to the League of Nations, prophesying that in six years we would witness a considerable reduction in armaments. He should have said in ninety-nine years: the danger of being wrong would have been less. And I am still wondering on what he bases his prophecy?
Therefore, backed by facts and common sense, while acknowledging the honesty, hon-ourability, earnestness and good faith of our delegates, I state that it is not less true, that the part played by the League of Nations-apart from questions of a sociological order, which each nation can settle at home- amounts to introducing resolutions which have no force, forming committees, sub-committees and super-committees, commissions, sub-commissions and super-commissions maintaining a staff of secretaries, assistant secretaries, private or public, stenographers type-writers, from class A to C, translators in as many languages as there are nationalities; having printed similarly in as many languages, documents the last of which has no more value than the first and is hardly worth the paper on which they are printed. Within the last twelve years, a bevy of young aristocrats associated with a few old parliamentarians, has sprung up in Europe, at a cost of $300,000 per year representing our contribution in an effort to suppress common sense and substituting in its place perpetual motion. This joke, at Geneva, has already lasted too long, and it behooves the government to cease participating in the League of Nations; such expenses, should no longer be defrayed by taxes levied on the Canadian people.
It seems that the more the question of armament crops up, the more this cancer spreads in all spheres; we even come across traces of it in the policy of this government. For instance, apart from the new taxation, the salaries of all civil servants have been cut ten per cent, except those who bear arms in the country's defence in peace time. 139 officers receive a salary from $4,000 to S4,900 ;	30
receive a salary from $6,000 to $6,900; mostly military bureaucrats, apart from an army of a few hundred men detailed to escort the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), and the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) when they leave to attend the Disarmament conference, Oh, irony of fate! on behalf of peace and security. These defensors of Parliament Hill are exempt from the ten per cent cut. This exemption is unfair to the other civil servants and meets with our disapproval.

A
third point to which I want to draw the attention of the government and make some suggestions, is the amendment to the Customs Act enacted on June 11, 1928, in connection with alcohol traffic between Canada and the United States. The government of that day wishing to keep up good relations with our neighbours, amended the Customs Act, chapter 16 George V of the Revised Statutes, so as to facilitate to the United States the task of enforcing their regulations.
From that date the Canadian government kept its word as regards fits preventive service staff, paid from the treasury funds, pursuant to *the act and to the benefit of our neighbours. The liquor industry, in Canada, fell short by about $20,000,000, on which we lost the excise tax; in return, our neighbours, to repay our kindness, thought proper to close their markets to practically all our products, by erecting a prohibitive tariff wall. Liquor traffic is recognized as legal in Canada; it is carried on under the regulations of our governments, and cannot be looked upon as an immoral trade; we therefore should not hesitate to cancel this act which makes Canada play a deceitful part. I submit, sir, that the amendment to the Customs Act, chapter 16 George V, Article 151 and the following in our Revised Statutes should be cancelled, leaving to our neighbours the full task of enforcing their regulations within the limits of their territory so far as spirits are concerned, just as the}' do in regard to foreign products which cross their border.
After all, this change is only right, because we should not tax the Canadians, in these hard times, to please others. I feel convinced that should my suggestions be adopted, the federal treasury would be the richer and the country would greatly benefit thereby.
Mr. J.-E. TETREAULT (Shefford) (Translation) :	Mr. Speaker, I feel greatly awed in
rising for the first time, in the house, as the representative of the county of Shefford. I avail myself of this opportunity, to thank my constituents for the honour they bestowed upon me by electing me to represent this beautiful county.

speechtext:
I say:
This beautiful county. Indeed, the county of Shefford has been highly honoured in the past, thanks to the fame of its renowned politicians and distinguished speakers who represented the county in the parliament of
The Budget-Mr. Tetreault

Canada. To mention but a few names, I shall recall to your memory those of the Hon. Mr. Huntington and the Hon. Mr. Boivin who were its representatives, the former from 1867 to 1878, and the latter from 1911 to 1925.
These two men proved themselves worthy of the two great races of this country and were numbered among the leaders of their day.
Being only a newcomer, sir, I do not harbour the illusion that I represent the county with as much authority as did these two hon. gentlemen. However, if devotion to duty and work mean anything, my constituents will know that they did not bestow this trust in vain and the future will bear evidence that I endeavoured to deserve it.
I am pleased to state, at the outset of my remarks, that if I have been elected, it is because we had as leader of our party one of the greatest statesmen that Canada has so far produced, and that the policy he advocates could, alone, extricate our country from the old beaten path where the previous regime had led it.
My friends opposite have not yet realized this, but the future will prove to them that there was but one effective policy, and that was the policy which gives protection to our industries, our trade and our farm products.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), was placed in power, thanks to his motto of ''Canada First"-our hon. friends opposite reminded him of it often enough. He gave proof at the Imperial conference, that it was not an empty election cry.
The Social Labour party which was for a time at the head of the most Conservative country in the world, lost for a moment the sense of British traditions, it failed, as communism is failing in another Conservative country: Russia.
England, however, needed a vigorous Conservative impulse to make her realize her situation and it came, for the first time, from the outside. It was the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada, who, at the Imperial conference, was to write down the historical page of this impulse.
Mr. Speaker, as I wish to be understood by all the members of this house, I beg of my French speaking colleagues to allow me to continue my remarks in English.
Mr. Speaker, I claim the indulgence of hon. members as I -rise to make my maiden speech in this house. Although it was not my intention to speak at this time, I feel it my duty to make a few remarks concerning the attitude of some hon. members on the other side of the house. I have listened attentively to the debate, and I wonder if any hon. member

opposite has said one word in favour of the government. Of course it does not surprise me that they should not do so, because I know the kind of cooperation we receive in the province of Quebec. Hon. members who had the opportunity to listen to Liberal speeches during the last provincial election campaign will readily appreciate the type of cooperation the Prime Minister may expect to receive from hon. members opposite. We have heard them criticize everything the present government has done. Why can they not be sincere and tell the truth to the people of Canada? I should like to tell hon. members what this government has done for my own town of Granby. Before going further may I say that we have had the cooperation of every citizen in that town, regardless of -political views. The people have worked together when the interests of our town were at stake.
Mr. ST-PERE: Nobody denies that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thanks to the tariff changes, we have attracted four new industries to our town. I am proud to say that we are the only town with a population of
10,000	which has succeeded in making such progress, and our success was partly due to the cooperation of the board of trade and the Southern Canada Power Company.
Mr. ST-PERE: They do not charge too much for their gas?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No more than they do in Montreal. If hon. members opposite do not appreciate the efforts this government is making, I am in a position to prove that in the county of Shefford we have some intelligent citizens who do appreciate them.
With your permission Mr. Speaker I should like to quote from a few letters I have received from people in my constituency since this government took office. In these letters are emphasized the benefits received from the policy of protection adopted by the leader of this government.
The first letter is dated September 27, 1930, and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Tetreault,
1 have your -letter of the 20th instant with reference to the new change in tariff.
I am thoroughly convinced that the present government has made a wonderful move which will result in far better business conditions in the Dominion of Canada. There are undoubtedly certain items which will have to be readjusted in the carte blanche program they have put through, but so far as our particular industry is concerned, it is just what we needed.
You might be interested to know that in view of this tariff, we are planning to put up an addition which will double our output. This will not only give work to contractors and

The Budget-Mr. Tetreault
labourers in the building of our plant, but will also enable me to employ considerably more hands in the near future.
This past week I have been visiting the retail trade in western Ontario, and find them, in every instance, quite pleased with the fact that we are getting an additional protection on our merchandise. I have convinced them that even though there may be a slight increase in the cost of our rayon yarns in the near future, I do not intend to raise iqy prices, and that I am in hopes with the added protection to be able to decrease my prices in the near future.
On the whole, I think the present government deserves a great deal of credit, and it is through the cooperation of such firms as ours who are not raising their prices, and who will decrease prices if at all possible, that their policy will succeed-
For your further information, you will no doubt be pleased to note that due to the protection given the corset manufacturers, each of them is looking for an increased business and placed orders with us this past week far in excess of yardages ever procured before.
With kindest regards, and my best wishes for the success of the present policy, I am Yours very truly,
Carl Stohn of Canada, Limited.
Then I have the following letter dated April 25, 1931:
Dear Mr. Tetreault:
I have your letter of the 22nd with reference to the improvement on our plant since last September.
For your information, beg to advise that immediately upon receipt of the news that a new tariff had been brought into effect on last September, the writer called a directors' meeting of our firm, and within ten days' time a contract was let for the building of an additional 27,000 square feet to our present plant. On October the 10th the contractors started to break ground in preparation of the starting of the building. Orders for additional machinery etc., were immediately placed and up to the present writing we have expended approximately $200,000 in building and machinery. Needless to say, our payroll has increased considerably and we are now employing approximately 160 hands, whereas last September, we were employing 92 hands. Our payroll has increased approximately 35 per cent in dollars and cents.
It is very interesting indeed to note our increased sales in spite of the general poor conditions throughout the country. Up to the end of March, our sales increased approximately 37 per cent over and above the first quarter of 1930, and we might say that 1930 was the best year in our business. We can definitely trace orders which have come to us which would have been placed in the United States had it not been for the increased tariff.
Thanking you for your kind interest, we beg to remain,
Yours very truly,
Carl Stohn of Canada, Limited.
On September 18, 1930, I received this letter from the Granby Manufacturing Company Limited:
Dear Eugene:
Mr. Carl Stohn was in our shop yesterday and we discussed the new tariff. He states that the new duty on textile will be of the greatest assistance to them. In fact he went so far as to state that they intended to build a new factory to look after the increased business-
I thought you might be pleased to hear the above and might have an opportunity to give Mr. Bennett at least one example of the results of his Canada-first policy.
Yours truly,
N. E. Clouston.
On June 4, 1931, the Atlas Plywood Corporation, Waterloo, Quebec, wrote me:
Dear Sir,
We received yours of the 3rd with list of new tariff enclosed which certainly comes pretty near to what we were asking for.
We wish to thank you sincerely for the part you took in this matter for us and for all the trouble you have been to. Can promise you that when the occasion arises again you can rely on us in every way.
On June 8, 1931, the manager of the corporation wrote me this second letter:
Dear Sir,
Thanks very much for the booklet you sent me. I am forwarding this on to our Boston office and am also enclosing your letter and am telling them that you, personally, are the one who assisted us in getting what we asked for.
And again on February 24 of this year the Atlas corporation wrote me the following letter:
Dear Sir,
Replying to yours of the 17th instant in reference to the new tariff of veneers, would say that the change has certainly been a benefit to our company.
In 1931 we had from 45 to 60 employees and paid per month $3,539.40 and made shipments of 615,739 feet per month, while in 1932 we have had continually from 65 to 70 employees, paying $4,117.17 per month and shipping 910.695 feet per month, so by these figures you can see we have benefited by the tariff.
If there is any further information that we can give you please let us know, and in the meantime we wish to thank you for the many courtesies you have .shown us since you have been in Ottawa.
On May 21, 1931, the Macdonald Metal Products Company Limited, Waterloo, Quebec, wrote me this letter:
Dear Mr. Tetreault,
Your letter of May 19th has been received, and we certainly appreciate the activity which you are taking in regard to our products.
You will be pleased to learn that our factory is running on practically the same basis as it was this time last year, due entirely in our estimation to the department's increase of tariff on nickel-plated goods, particularly our line of nickel-plated cake turners, mixing spoons, and other kitchen utensils. The effect of last fall's increase in this tariff item has made it possible for us to manufacture just as many articles in
The Budget-Mr. Tetreault

this poor year as we did last year, and has not increased the cost of these articles to the consumer one cent.
They wrote me again under date of June 3, 1931:
Dear Mr. Tetreault,
We are quite pleased to note in the various changes in the budget that the item dolls and toys of all kinds has been raised from 30 per cent to 40 per cent duty. We believe that this is going to make a tremendous difference in our business here, and we wish to thank you at this time very much for the effort that you have put in at Ottawa on our behalf. We believe also that this 10 per cent increase will greatly discourage the importation of German cap pistols. A few of the items that we import through necessity have been increased in cost on account of the budget, but we are quite content with these increases as no doubt they are designed to help other manufacturers.
That is what we call cooperation.
You will be quite pleased, I am sure, to know that our sales to date this year are practically the same as they were last year, and also that we attribute this to the increase of the duty put through last fall on nickel-plated goods. Also in this connection, we would advise that instead of our prices going up on account of the increased duty there have been a number of changes downward.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): This does not contain letters from unemployed?

speechtext:
Neither is it due to the opposition.
On February 9, 1932, I received another letter from the Macdonald Metal Products Company, Limited, of which I will give the house the concluding paragraph:
We -wish to have you convey to the Prime Minister our thanks for the various protective changes made last year, and advise him that we operated about one-third more time last year than wre did in 1930, and that this year we expect to operate practically to full capacity throughout the year, which should mean about a full 50 per cent better than 1930 operations.
The next letter I am going to read is not from a manufacturer, but from a firm engaged in growing mushrooms. They say.
Dear Sir:
We have just received a circular from the horticultural council at Ottawa informing us that the department had placed a minimum value of 30 cents per pound on mushrooms for import. In consequence this will fix this matter up in a thoroughly satisfactory manner for ourselves. as the dump duty applies on anything brought in below this value.
[Mr. Tetreault.l
We wish to thank you for the trouble you have taken for us in this matter, and will endeavour to do whatever we can for you at any time.
Yours very truly,
Slack Brothers,
The next letter is in French. This too is not from a big manufacturing firm, but from a man engaged in making charcoal:
Flodden, Que., June 5, 1931. Mr. J. E. Tetrault, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-[DOT]
My most sincere thanks and congratulations on your success as regards the tariff on charcoal. The new tariff will have as an immediate result the reopening of factories and the building of new plants which will employ 2,500 men.
My employees as well as the farmers who sell me wood join with me in expressing our thanks and congratulations.
Yours gratefully,
Ovila Pratte.
I have received from another newly established industry, a letter which demonstrates that these new companies recognize that they are receiving cooperation from this government. It reads:
We have your letter of March 16th, enclosing a copy of the commissioner's letter of March 14th, relative to William Wagner.
Will you please express to Mr. Joliffe our sincere appreciation of his cooperation in allowing us to bring in the different helpers that we required from our other mill.
Mr. J. W. Stark and the writer both feel that there has been a real understanding of our problems, and the promptness with which our requests were granted has been most gratifying.
It is very apparent that our needs have been most promptly and clearly placed before the commissioner, and it is therefore again a great pleasure to thank you most heartily for your service in looking after us so thoroughly and well.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Is that the end?

speechtext:
The article is as follows:
Normal Times Return
The Dominion Statistics of Trade and Commerce show a favourable balance of $15,000,000 for the period of the eleven months of the fiscal year just ended. It is a sign of the times of which we can rejoice, since it indicates a movement towards the reestablishment of the economic equilibrium in the Dominion. Our exports are in excess of our imports, that is we sell more than we buy. We consume still more home products, and this is all to the advantage of Canadian producers, as well as to that of the consumers themselves.
These are not the views expressed by members on the opposition side.
A country which is self-sufficing, which produces at home what it requires, instead of purchasing it abroad, is economically independent and its political life is less subject to changes.
A recent report of Mr. Frederick Hudd, Canadian Trade Commissioner in New York, gives interesting facts on trade dealings between Canada and the United States. Although, he states, the United States exports to Canada and the imports of Canada from the United states have shown a large decrease, in volume as well as in value, the largest decrease is found in United States exports. The latter total $395,647,609 in 1931, compared to $659,093,588 in 1930, therefore a decrease of $269,296,780 or 39-9 per cent. On the other hand, the Canadian imports from the United States amounted to $266,296,780 compared with $402,350,280 in 1930, a decrease of $136,053,509 or 33*81 per cent. Briefly, the unfavourable balance of trade of Canada with the United States totalled $139,350,821, in 1931, instead of $256,743,308. as in 1930.
Mr. Hudd points out a few groups of products on which the variations of Canadian-American international trade was more marked. As regards agricultural products, the value of Canadian corn exports amounted to $1,181,829 compared with $4,179,489, in 1930, and that of raw cotton was $7,247,434, instead of $13,051,040. As to the group of mineral products, the value of the U nited States exports of bituminous coal to Canada came to $37,624,093 compared to $49,981,697 in 1930. Crude oil and gasoline as well as manufactured metal products still show a greater decrease. The same can be said of United States imports of cheese, cattle hides, furs, linseed, unbleached sulphite paste, newspaper, non-eoncentrated copper, lead ore and lead matts.
However, the imports of bleached sulphite paste and concentrated cupriferous articles have greatly increased.
As a whole, our trade balance with the neighbouring republic tends to improve, while our trade with Great Britain, Australia, New 41761-135
18, 1932	2145
The Budget-Mr. Tetreault
Zealand and the other countries of the Empire give rise to great promises. There are encouraging prospects which portend to normal economic conditions for the future and therefore the end of the present crisis in a still nearer future.
My hon. friends will note that it is La Presse which makes this statement.
If hon. members opposite do not believe that the government is taking the proper means to solve the great problems facing this country, they can find the proof in the statement which appeared in La Presse.
I have mentioned what this government has done for industry and trade, and I should like now to draw the attention of all the government members to the situation confronting our farmers. The exact position in which the farmers of this country now find themselves may not be realized, but they know that the government is ready to cooperate to the fullest extent with the provincial governments in order to improve their position. I submit that the Quebec government, with its surplus dating back many years, should come to the rescue of the farmers of that province. The system of farm loans has been found to be nearly useless as far as Quebec is concerned, as only fourteen per cent of the loans applied for have been granted. It is not fair to help only fourteen per cent of the farmers and let the rest starve. If I am to be allowed to make a suggestion to the farm loan board, it would be that changes be made at once which would enable the farmers to obtain the amounts they urgently require. Hon. members opposite have been criticizing the government for not properly taking care of the farmer, and we should all work together, provincially and federally, to try to relieve the situation of agriculture. As things are going just now, conditions will be bad for the farmers this fall and some plan should be evolved to give required assistance to the farmers of Quebec and the other provinces.
I should like now to refer to a question of mine which appeared on the order paper for February 15 concerning the number of married women in the service of the government. It was a great surprise to me to learn that seventy-four of these women were not living with their husbands. I believe that the cause of this is that they have a position which enables them to be independent. I have received many letters from married women who protest against the employment of other married women who are not living with their husbands. I should not like all married women to believe that I am an enemy of women because I have a wife of my own who is certainly my best friend. However, in

The Budget-Mr. Arsenault

times of depression we certainly should give preference to the married man who has a wife and family to support. The government should investigate the matter, and if there are any cases where the father of a family could be employed instead of some married woman who is not the sole support of a family, then let such a man be employed.
Since I have a few minutes more I want to read now an article from the Canadian Textile Journal, with reference to Manhattan Mills Limited:
Manhattan Mills Ltd. Establish Rayon Weaving Plant at Granby
144 Loom Plant to be Brought from Taunton,
Mass. New Building to be Erected at Once
Another new textile industry for Canada was announced the latter part of March, The Manhattan Mills Limited, manufacturers of rayon and silk dress materials.
They have decided to locate in Granby, Que., where a new factory, 70 ft. x 240 ft. one storey brick and cement construction, will be built at once and it is hoped to complete the building within two months.
The new company starts off under unusually strong conditions. Mr. Harry Altman who will assume personal direction of the new company is well knovm as being thoroughly capable in this line having many years of practical experience in making fine dress goods. Their selling organization in Canada is already well established as the Manhattan Silk and Woollens Limited, of Montreal and Toronto, who have achieved success as wholesalers and jobbers in this line, are merging their interest with the new company.	.
The coming of this company to Canada is different from most companies in that instead of this being a branch of an American firm, in this case the entire factory consisting of 144 looms and other necessary complementing machinery will be moved entirely to Granby from Taunton, Mass., where it has been operating.
Textile and Industrial Centre
Granby was selected as the location for the new factory after investigating a great many sites, and should prove a happy choice, as this city has become well known as an exceptionally fine manufacturing city, as the many diversified industries successfully operating there bear witness. In the textile trades in Granby are, The Granby Elastic Web Co. Limited, The Esmond Mills Inc., Carl Stohn of Canada Limited. The Nordic Hosiery Limited, Stark Bros. Ribbon Corp. of Canada, while other large industries outside of the textile group located in Granby are, The Miner Rubber Co. Limited, The Imperial Tobacco Co. Limited, The Stedfast Rubber Co., Giddings Limited, reed and rattan furniture, The Meyer Thomas Co. Limited, box manufacturers, Granby Last Company. The Granby Manufacturing Co. Limited, makers of celluloid tees and novelties, United Maple Products Limited, Barre & Charron. interior woodwork, Kent Lumber Co., Albert Morin Mattress Factory, James Topp Cigar Co., and many other smaller industries.
Several of the above factories outside of the textile group use large quantities of textiles,
[Mr. 'KtreaultJ
such as the Miner Rubber Co. Limited, Giddings Limited, Stedfast Rubber Co. and others.
Work on transferring the Manhattan mills to Granby will be rushed with all possible speed and it is hoped to have this factory ready for operation within three months.
Such a record was made when the Stark Bros. Ribbon Corp. opened in Granby late last fall, as they were delivering ribbon three months after they decided to open a factory in Granby.
The Manhattan mills expect to employ about 150 people when they commence operations.
Before resuming my seat, I should like to assure hon. members that we from Quebec are proud to have in that province a large number of English speaking people. In my own constituency we have about twenty per cent English speaking, and in the town of Granby the two races are getting along wonderfully.
Mr. St-PERE: We are getting along very well.

speechtext:
In my constituency
French Canadians and English Canadians are working hand in hand, and it is only by means of such cooperation that we can hope to build up this beloved Canada of ours.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to say a few words on the question before the house, I am aware of the difficult task that faces a new member when, from a sense of duty towards those whom he represents, he undertakes for the first time to address himself to his colleagues in the House of Commons, many of whom have had many years of parliamentary experience. Coming from a county where the majority of the population are of French descent, I think it is proper-and I believe the house will agree with me-that I should express myself in the beautiful language with which I am more familiar.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend my sincerest congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), not only on the high office he so worthily fills today, but also for his clear and concise statement on the economic situation of Canada which he has so well explained in the budget, and which lucidly defines our revenues, liabilities and expenditures. Speaking on behalf of the citizens of Kent county, who have entrusted me with a mandate' in this parliament, I also wish to add my token to the great mark of confidence of which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is at present the object, for the courage, ability and earnestness he displays in the great crisis

The Budget-Mr. Belec
we are going through. While that crisis is world-wide in its effect, it, however, places upon us serious obligations and duties, a difficult and ungrateful task. We have faith in the future, and the country's affairs could not be in better hands than those of the man whom all acknowledge to be honest, highly experienced and well versed in financial matters. I refer to the right hon. Prime Minister. _ In previous debates, the Liberals unceasingly reminded the Prime Minister of his pledges to the electorate during the last election. They seem to ignore that the situation we have to face to-day has been greatly aggravated by uncontrollable causes. They forget that the gates have been closed to immigration in order to keep unemployment at its lowest ebb; that the raising of the tariff resulted in preventing our markets from being flooded by foreign products, thus keeping the Canadian markets for our own producers when times become more favourable. They further forget that the obligations contracted in times of prosperity, the changes brought about by the motor car and its greater perfection, are as many burdens which weigh more and more, add to this the hardships prevailing, accustomed as we were to living somewhat in comfort. Hence these fixed charges such as the enormous amount entailed in the pensions to veterans, the interest on the national debt and the necessary maintenance of our national railways. These new burdens have greatly increased owing to the world wide crisis, and they thrust upon us the pressing duty to economize instead of distributing favours, to cut down salaries instead of increasing them; to reduce the number of civil servants instead of enlarging it. Now, sir, addressing myself to the people of Kent county, mostly fishermen or farmers, I wish to assure them that their special interests have not been lost sight of by the federal authorities who are aware that the fisheries and the farm are, in our section of the country, the two main industries. To the farmers of my county, I shall repeat what, the other day, the president of the French Canadian Association on Education stated to the French Canadian Agricultural Association of Ontario: while certain members of the family-under the guidance of the father and mother, heads of the establishment -will produce grain, fodder, vegetables, other members will busy themselves with making clothes, others will look after the fruit, the preserving of food, the making of cheese and butter, still others will utilize their time in making and repairing furniture, vehicles, sledges, farm implements and erecting and repairing the buildings. So that each member 41761-1351
of the family will have work distributed to him according to his age, abilities and fitness. Every one being thus interested in his task, knowing that he is working for himself and his family, will not think of leaving the locality, where he finds continuous and remunerative work, to go to the city or the mills, where the assurance of work and remuneration become daily more uncertain. It is true, that for a number of years, the whole economic organization of this country has tended to destroy home industries and to commercialize certain branches of agriculture. The result is that our rural districts are short of money which is constantly being drained to other centres. All agricultural branches which have been exclusively industrialized have been the cause of over production and have ruined many a rural family who had followed such practice. For ininstance, the wheat growers who realized large profits as long as their products found an easy market, but the moment the wheat market fell, distress replaced abundance among this class of farmers who have specialized in one branch of agriculture without paying any attention- to providing clothes or food products for family consumption.
As to the fishermen of the county of Kent, I wish to inform them that the federal Minister of Fisheries is alert to all which may interest them and, if the present depression is hard on them, they must not lose faith, but hope that their lot will soon improve.
To these two groups, as well as to others, I wish to extend the assurance of my sincere sympathy and unceasing zeal for all that concerns and interests them.
In closing my remarks, let me once more express to the people of the beautiful county of Kent my very sincere thanks for the honour they have bestowed upon me by electing me as their representative. I wish to assure them that on all occasions I shall deem it my duty to protect the special interests of my county and the country at large.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my address may I follow the excellent example of those who have preceded me in this debate, and extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) upon the excellent manner in which he has explained the budget to parliament and the country. The budget is a businesslike statement which clearly sets forth Canada's high position among the nations of the world. It shows how Canada has balanced -her trade, met all her obligations and maintained her credit. The government of which I am a supporter has courageously tackled the
The Budget-Mr. Belec

unemployment problem and thus brought relief to thousands of Canadian people. The budget has been well received by the country: it has not disturbed business and it has shown that, despite the world economic crisis, our position is relatively better off than that of any other country.
The tax levies in the budget have been placed on those best able to bear them, and will not prove a hardship to the farmer who in these days has problems of his own. 1 should also like to remind the house that the government has saved our country industrially by enacting proper tariff protection. As a result of the tariff policy of the Bennett government more than 157 new industries have been established in Canada since the last-dominion election, and they are employing Canadian men and women who were idle during the latter years of Liberal misrule.
I should like to tell the house something of the county which I have the honour to represent in this parliament. Pontiac is undergoing the stress of hard times, but undergoing it with courage. The people of that county are descendants of sturdy pioneer stock who have contributed so much to our country. Pontiac is going through the depression, but is not going back. It is true that lumbering, which has been one of our basic industries, is not what it has been in the past, but in agriculture and mining my county is second to none in this or any other country. Think of the diversified wealth in Pontiac. We have the rich Rouyn gold area with the great Noranda mine, while in the Abitibi district the discovery of rich ores presages great development. At Timiskaming we have the great plant of the International Paper Company. In regard to lumbering, may I say that we have untold resources in pulp and hardwood. As a matter of fact the only virgin pine in Quebec is to be found in Pontiac around Grand Lake Victoria.
The constituency of Pontiac extends from the town of Aylmer on the Ottawa river to James bay, and is one of the largest in area in Canada. We have the resources, but best of all, we have the people. The census taken in June of last year shows the population of Pontiac to be 64,155, which represents a gain of nearly 20.000 since the last census was taken in 1921. This is the healthiest sign of all that our county is increasing by leaps and bounds. The northern part, Abitibi, has increased enormously; it has a population of 22,133, which is almost 10,000 more than ten years ago. The people of the northern end of my county, like the people of old Pontiac, depend not upon doles but upon themselves; they are workers, the best in the country.

As regards financial matters, may I say that old Pontiac is out of debt as far as county rates are concerned, and most of the municipalities are in the same happy position. My own municipality of Mansfield does not owe a dollar. I have been a member of the Mansfield council for thirty-five years, mayor for fifteen years and, besides that, chairman of the school board for years. In Pontiac we pay our way. Our people are not extravagant, but limit their spending to their means.
I should now like to say something about agricultural conditions in my county. Prices, in common with those the world over, are the lowest in years, and I would respectfully urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) to include Pontiac in the schemes of departmental activity. I regret to say that under the previous government our county was neglected, and, may I say, ignored. I often hear the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) speaking in the house, but I find that during his administration the Department of Agriculture did absolutely nothing for the farmers of Pontiac.	.
May I point out some of the agricultural resources of my county? The last census of live stock shows the following for Pontiac-I will deal with the Abitibi district first: horses, 2,877; cattle, 11,631; sheep, 1,651; swine, 4,461; poultry, 56,900. In Timiskaming the total live stock is as follows: horses, 2,934; cattle, 21,908; sheep, 10,130; swine, 7,581; poultry, 50,028. In old Pontiac there were 7,606 horses; 38,929 cattle; 25,844 sheep; 15,746 swine, and 162,770 poultry. Thus' the live stock census of 1931 showed the following for the whole county: horses, 13,417; cattle, 72,658; sheep, 28,625; swine, 27,688; poultry, 269,698. I have quoted these figures from the Bureau of Statistics to show that our country is progressing despite the hard times. But what we want is a market for our products. I would like to endorse the suggestion that was made by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), that mixed farming be encouraged by means of a cash bonus. This is an emergency situation, and such a step would bring great relief to the farmers of Pontiac county, who are all engaged in mixed farming. I believe that if our exports of live beef were bonused by two cents a pound it would greatly increase production and as well restore the purchasing power of the farmer. In this regard may I point out that the farmers of Canada represent forty-six per cent of the total population of the country, and until their purchasing power is restored general prosperity cannot return.
I would like to see the farmers of Canada recapture the bacon market in Great Britain, and to help them in accomplishing this the

government might grant an export bonus of two cents per pound. Denmark now enjoys the bacon market of Great Britain. In 1930 Denmark sold millions of pounds of bacon to Great Britain while we sold only a fraction of that amount. I would also respectfully urge the government to give the farmers a bonus on cheese and dairy products, and a bonus of say three -cents per dozen on eggs. This would bring prosperity to the farmer. Establishing a bonus system for our exportable farm surplus would automatically stimulate the market at home and return about $30,000,000 to the farmers of Canada through the increase in the price of farm products. The prices of farm products have dropped fifty per cent, and I -would respectfully suggest that it is time that something be done for the farmer.
We are looking forward -with the keenest anticipation to the Imperial conference to be held in Ottawa this summer, which I am sure will result in a marked stimulus to empire trade, bring about mutual advantages to the various parts of -the British Empire, and herald the return to better days and prosperity.
